articles.title: Vivek Ramaswamy discontinues attack ad that prompted wave of revulsion
articles.summary:
Candidate for Ohio governor confirms campaign no longer airing ad that smeared rival and was defended by Trump

Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican nominee for Ohio governor, confirmed on…

blocks.text: Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican nominee for Ohio governor, confirmed on Thursday that his campaign is no longer airing an attack ad that features the estranged mother of his Democratic opponent, Amy Acton.

The ad prompted a wave of revulsion since Acton’s mother, Donna Arthur, lost custody of her daughter in 1978, when her second husband, Cledith Arthur, was charged with raping her daughter between the ages of 10 and 12.
Asked by a reporter in Vandalia, Ohio if his campaign had stopped running the ad, Ramaswamy said: “It ran to completion and we put up four other ads.”

“But what I will say is that for all of the discussion around 30-second ads, I would love, even for this final close, for this campaign to really be about policy,” Ramaswamy added, before criticizing his opponent for not debating him.

Ramaswamy’s campaign had announced last week that it would spend $4m to broadcast the ad, despite criticism from Democrats and Republicans after court records showed that Acton’s mother, who called her daughter “a liar”, had fled the state with her husband when her daughter accused him of rape.

In an interview with the anti-abortion group Operation Rescue in 2020, when Acton was leading Ohio’s response to the Covid pandemic, Acton’s mother said that she was aware that, before she married him, Cledith Arthur had previously been accused of raping his own daughter.

Ramaswamy’s reference to “30-second ads” referred to the length of the ad after his campaign edited the original 60-second version, to remove the allegation from Acton’s mother that her daughter had lied about the family having lived in a tent with Arthur when she was a child.
Court records from the time indicated that Cledith Arthur had, indeed, lived in a tent at the time of his arrest on rape charges.

Donald Trump repeatedly defended the ad, including at a rally with Ramaswamy on Wednesday, while refusing to acknowledge that the serious child rape allegation was relevant to the credibility of Acton’s mother.

Reporting from NBC News and Zeteo suggests that Acton’s mother has suffered from mental health challenges and was found living in her car with dozens of cats, which troubled some people involved in producing the ad for Ramaswamy’s campaign.

“How far will Vivek Ramaswamy go?” Acton’s campaign asked in a new ad on the controversy released earlier on Thursday. “To become governor, he’ll smear his opponent for being raped by her stepfather when she was just 10 years old – exploiting the sexual abuse of a child and spending millions lying to you about it,” the ad warns Ohio voters.

Acton also addressed Ramaswamy’s attack ad at an event on Thursday. “You’ve probably all heard by now, if you didn’t know, a little bit about my childhood,” she told supporters. “My brother and I experienced a lot of things, a lot of abuse and a lot of neglect. We were frequent flyers in children’s services, ended up living in a tent in the middle of winter.”

“My opponent has now chosen to exploit my childhood intentionally,” she continued. “He’s doing it in a desperate attempt to save his struggling campaign. But I’ll tell you, Mr Ramaswamy, it’s not going to work.”

articles.title: Binance crypto platform suspends trades amid suspected hack
articles.summary: The platform suspended some trading while crypto companies froze billions in their respective currencies. The full extent of the possible hack was not yet clear.

image.caption: Binance has the largest volume of daily trading out of any crypto platformImage: Silas Stein/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The world's largest cryptocurrency platform, Binance, confirmed on Thursday that it was investigating a potential security breach.
"It does look like a hack on Binance," said former company chief Changpeng Zhao, who remains a major shareholder.
Some $2.5 billion (€2.8 billion) had been frozen in response to the suspected hack.
"Rest assured that user funds are completely safe," a company spokesperson said.
Binance 'reviewing' possible hack
The extent of the possible security breach was not immediately disclosed. Binance did not say whether any cryptocurrency funds had been stolen.

"Our security teams are reviewing all relevant information with urgency, and we will provide updates through official Binance channels as soon as we have verified information," the company statement said.
How to avoid crypto losses

The company, which is the world's largest platform in terms of daily crypto trading volume, suspended trading on certain products while the freezing came from cryptocurrency companies using the platform.
Tether froze around $1.6 billion in its USDT currency, according to CEO Paolo Ardoino, and Circle froze some $800 million-worth of USDC, boss Jeremy Allaire said.
Who is Binance ex-CEO Zhao?
The news of the possible hack sent Bitcoin's value tumbling by 3.2% on Thursday evening, dropping below $79,000.
Zhao, who founded the Binance platform in 2017, said "as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered."
He stepped down as CEO after pleading guilty in 2023. to failing to prevent money laundering on his platform. US President Donald Trump pardoned him in 2025.
Zhao and Binance have been key supporters of cryptocurrency ventures by US President Donald Trump and his family.

articles.title: Antisemitism envoy proposes ‘external ombudsman’ to monitor ABC and SBS coverage of Israel and Middle East
articles.summary:
Jillian Segal says perception of link between coverage of conflicts and hostility towards Jewish Australians ‘is itself a matter of public importance’

  • Get our

blocks.text: The federal government’s anti-semitism envoy has proposed an “external independent ombudsman” to monitor ABC and SBS coverage of the war in Gaza, as well as codes for arts organisations to limit “personal political or ideological activism”.
In an updated plan released on Friday, Jillian Segal said Australia’s two public broadcasters should be subjected to greater oversight.

“Given the extent and seriousness of concerns about subjective, inaccurate and disproportionate reporting in accordance with its own standards, it would be in the public interest for the public broadcasters’ coverage and approach to be the subject of more detailed analysis and independent review,” Segal wrote in the new ASECA Priorities plan.

It suggests a government-appointed panel review the public broadcasters’ previous reporting and states the government should consider “transferring” responsibilities from the ABC and SBS ombudsmen. Those powers would be transferred to an “external independent ombudsman consistent with other sectors such as telecommunications and banking”.

“Many in the Jewish community remain concerned that coverage they perceive as one-directional may contribute to a negative – and even hostile – view by audiences of those who support Israel, or have sympathy for it,” Segal writes.
“Jewish Australians have reported being abused, harassed and accused of being ‘baby killers’ or supporters of ‘genocide’ simply for their belief in the right of Israel to exist.
“That perception of a link between coverage and hostility is itself a matter of public importance.”

Segal said she had received “many expressions of concern from the Australian Jewish community” about ABC and SBS reporting that was perceived to be “disproportionate, misleading or inaccurate on issues relating to Israel and the conflict in the Middle East”.

The special envoy to combat antisemitism’s initial plan, released in mid-2025, said the envoy would “work with the publicly funded broadcasters to encourage them to develop programs that add to social cohesion”.
Segal then told the royal commission into antisemtism in mid-2026 she wanted a new “oversight” committee that could give ABC and SBS coverage a “tick” or “guidance”.
The broadcasters rejected calls for external oversight.
The royal commission was established in response to the Bondi beach massacre in December when 15 people were killed during a Hanukah celebration.
Segal appeared before Senate estimates this week, telling senators she held concerns about “the tone [and] the frequency of reporting about Gaza from the ABC”.
Friday’s report argues publicly funded arts organisations should be able to impose “enforceable conditions” on artists and terminate grants if they promoted antisemitism.

Segal states that all arts organisations – private and public – should develop policies to govern the use of their venues, festivals, and stages “or artists’ personal political or ideological activism outside the scope of the advertised show, performance or exhibition”.

Similarly for universities, the envoy’s updated plan proposes allowing grant authorities to impose enforceable conditions on academics, allowing “for the termination of grant funding … where the recipient engages in antisemitic speech or conduct”.
after newsletter promotion
Segal said the proposals outlined in the plan were “not about silencing criticism of Israel”.
The report argues that “modern ‘progressive’ antisemitism” was the most pervasive form of the prejudice in Australia today.

“It takes the hostility of Islamic extremism and far-left antisemitism, together with traditional antisemitic tropes, and gives it a respectable face through the language of social justice and human rights”.
Segal said Islamic extremism, far-left and far-right antisemitism were still prevalent “and they require vigilance and laws that are properly enforced”.

“But the form that is leaving Jewish Australians increasingly anxious and excluded is the one that has taken root in influential institutions, where Jewish Australians are being discriminated against, blamed and vilified for the actions of the government of the state of Israel.”
The release of the envoy’s updated plan comes two days after Segal appeared at Senate estimates.

She defended evidence she gave to the royal commission into antisemitism, during which she criticised SBS for quoting death toll figures provided by the Gaza Ministry of Health, saying those figures failed to distinguish combatants from civilians, were “grossly inflated” and their inflation was “well known and even accepted by the United Nations”.

A spokesperson for the UN secretary general responded at the time: “For us [the UN] the Ministry of Health in Gaza is a source we, and many others, often cite. Independent validation of subsets of the data has found no significant discrepancies in their numbers.”

Segal told the estimates hearing this week: “I note the United Nations views. I accept the United Nations views because they are the United Nations but that does not detract from the concerns of the Jewish community as conveyed to me about the way in which the reporting had been done.”

articles.title: [Market Rider] Things you may not know about Jinky Luistro
articles.summary: The outcome of Vice President Sara Duterte's impeachment trial will decide Luistro's political future

blocks.text: It was a beautiful Monday morning, bright and sunny. The traffic was surprisingly calm and smooth, even as pedestrians and vehicles were beginning to gather while I hurriedly made my way to the Monday Circle breakfast forum last October 26. This pleasant start to the week was a rare surprise these days.

But the day’s biggest surprise was yet to come. In an intimate, exclusive moment, the members and guests of the Monday Circle got a rare, behind-the-scenes look into the personal life and career of one of the country’s present most recognizable faces in politics: Batangas 2nd District Representative Gerville Abanilla “Jinky” Reyes-Luistro.

Luistro has drawn national attention through extensive media and television coverage especially for her prominent role as chairperson of the House committee on justice and lead prosecutor in the ongoing impeachment proceedings against Vice President Sara Duterte.

For Luistro, her entry into the political arena was less of a calculated career move but more of a choice to defend her family’s honor. In 2020, local rivals engineered a severe political hit against her husband, then-Mabini Mayor Noel “Bitrics” Luistro, filing two entirely fabricated counts of rape to derail his planned 2022 congressional run.

Forensic verification exposed the shocking truth. The alleged victims were completely fictitious entities cooked up by opponents. Local leaders and supporters urged her to carry the torch for their constituency, so that the seasoned lawyer stepped into the vacuum.
Embracing the province’s culture and values, she adopted the punchy moniker “Jinky Bitrics,” seamlessly balancing her identity as a family woman, legal advocate, and community leader.

Luistro carries a deep pride for her hometown of Mabini, Batangas — particularly the coastal enclave of Anilao. Globally celebrated as the “Nudibranch Capital of the World,” Anilao is a premier sanctuary for muck diving and underwater macro photography. It boasts of having the highest density and variety of nudibranchs on Earth. Unlike standard gastropod mollusks, these vibrant marine creatures are completely shell-less, showcasing a psychedelic array of neon colors and surreal patterns that look like real-life Pokémon to the international divers who flock there.
Much like the resilient, striking creatures of her native coast, Luistro has proven that a small profile can command global attention.

Long before walking the halls of the House of Representatives, Luistro built an extensive, battle-tested legal career. She earned a dual degree in Liberal Arts-Commerce and a Juris Doctor from the University of Batangas, passing the Philippine Bar Examinations in 2002.
While pursuing her legal studies, she simultaneously taught full-time as a professor at the Lyceum of Batangas and served as an executive assistant to then-justice secretary Hernando Perez.

Her subsequent legal practice spanned critical sectors of public service. She worked as a confidential agent for the Bureau of Immigration, a consultant for the Department of Justice’s Witness Protection Program, and a state counsel. Notably, under the Arroyo administration, she headed a high-stakes investigation for a Special Presidential Task Force probing systemic corruption within the Department of Finance.

Her good investigative work resulted in a landmark 2014 Supreme Court victory that firmly affirmed the dismissal of corrupt officials. Returning to her roots, she served as the municipal administrator of Mabini from 2016 to 2022, mastering the inner mechanics of local public administration.

Luistro launched her formal political career in 2022, winning a highly competitive congressional race for the 2nd District of Batangas by a razor-thin two-percentage-point margin against the incumbent’s daughter.

While she initially maintained a quiet profile, her sharp, razor-focused investigative skills during high-profile committee hearings quickly caught the eye of House leadership. Affiliated with the dominant Lakas-CMD party, she secured a resounding reelection victory in the May 2025 midterm elections. Her meteoric rise culminated in her historic appointment as the chairperson of the powerful House committee on justice, solidifying her status as the absolute legal authority in the chamber.

As chairperson of the justice committee, Luistro was selected to lead the 11-member House prosecution panel in the monumental Senate impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte. Thrust into the global spotlight, she bears the heavy burden of presenting evidence, orchestrating the overarching legal strategy, and directly cross-examining witnesses on the Senate floor.

Her stewardship of the historic trial reflects an aggressively tactical approach. On October 13, or 39 days on the impeachment trial, Luistro and her panel made the high-stakes decision to withdraw three of the four original articles of impeachment — dropping charges related to confidential funds, bribery, and grave threats in order to pivot entirely toward a single, robust charge: unexplained wealth.

Luistro clarified that this compression was a direct response to public impatience, designed to streamline the trial and dramatically shrink the defense’s presentation timeline, which is to commence on November 9.

Crucially, she emphasized that the dropped charges were not an acquittal; the prosecution panel intends to transfer their gathered evidence directly to the Office of the Ombudsman for independent criminal prosecution.

While this national trial has elevated Luistro to a household name, it places her political capital under immense strain. Her home district in Batangas is a traditional battleground of competing loyalties; leading an aggressive prosecution against a Duterte risks alienating conservative, pro-Duterte factions within her own constituency. Furthermore, she faces intense public scrutiny and stiff opposition from pro-Duterte senators who have threatened to stonewall or complicate the trial proceedings.

Luistro is acutely aware of the looming risk of personal and professional reprisal. She has publicly noted that while she is acting strictly under her constitutional mandate, the Vice President retains the right to counter-sue the prosecutors if acquitted — a reality for which Luistro states her team is fully prepared.

Also, the outcome of this impeachment trial will decide her political future. A successful conviction could solidify a path toward the Senate, while a failed trial could severely fracture her hard-earned local stronghold.

Now, Luistro finds herself standing on the fault line of a historic constitutional struggle. This role carries massive potential rewards for her national prominence, but it also carries significant risks to her accumulated political capital. Nevertheless, Luistro, is not intimidated by these risks that may serve as deciding factors to her political career, for what matters — in her own words — is the need to stand up for the preservation of the Constitution, love for country, the advancement of ethical conduct, transparency, accountability, and an effective catalyst for change.
Once more, the Monday Circle breakfast forum evolved into a captivating exchange of ideas and purpose with a fair lady, rising political architect and patriot. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Cebu, save your sensilyo! BSP’s coin machines could arrive by January 2027
articles.summary: After more than a year on pause, the central bank's popular coin deposit machines could return in January 2027, this time with a rollout beyond Metro Manila taking priority

blocks.text: Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas
After more than a year on pause, the central bank's popular coin deposit machines could return in January 2027, this time with a rollout beyond Metro Manila taking priority

items: The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) plans to reintroduce coin deposit machines by January 2027, with a focus on regional rollouts starting in Cebu.
The BSP aims to deploy 50 machines in total, 25 in Metro Manila and 25 in other regions, following the success of the initial launch in June 2023.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
Remember those coin deposit machines that let you turn your barya into digital cash? Well, they’re finally making a comeback, although a little later than expected.

In an interview with Rappler on the sidelines of the Bahandi launch, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) Deputy Governor Bernadette Romulo-Puyat said the central bank is now eyeing January 2027 for the machines’ return. The delay, she explained, has largely been due to the service provider taking longer than expected.
This time, the BSP wants a rollout across the regions first, with SM Cebu potentially getting first dibs.
“We’ll launch it in Cebu,” Romulo-Puyat told Rappler, adding that she also hopes to hold a launch in Mindanao.
The plan is to deploy 25 coin deposit machines outside the capital while also bringing back 25 machines in Metro Manila and doubling the original fleet.

After all, Metro Manila residents already had their turn when the BSP first introduced the machines in June 2023. (READ: How to turn coins into digital cash with Bangko Sentral’s coin deposit machines)

And what a hit they turned out to be. Filipinos hauled their loose change to participating malls, poured coins into the machines by the handful, and received the equivalent amount in their GCash or Maya wallets, GoTyme bank accounts, or shopping vouchers.
By March 2025, the BSP reported that the machines had collected around P1.4 billion worth of coins.
Now, the BSP is working with SM to bring them back, with the mall operator helping shoulder costs and identify high traffic locations for the machines.
Romulo-Puyat said the arrangement would help lower the cost of operating the program, which she acknowledged was expensive.

articles.title: ‘Star Trek’ and X-Men’ star Patrick Stewart dies at 86
articles.summary: He became Sir Patrick Stewart when he was knighted by the queen at Buckingham Palace in 2010

items: Patrick Stewart, the acclaimed actor known for his roles as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek and Professor Charles Xavier in X-Men, passed away at the age of 86 after a battle with Alzheimer's Disease and Lewy Body Dementia.
Stewart rose from a challenging childhood in England to achieve global fame, becoming a celebrated Shakespearean actor and later a key figure in major film franchises, including Star Trek and X-Men.
He was knighted in 2010 for his contributions to drama and is remembered for his significant impact on both theater and film, as well as for his personal journey of overcoming adversity.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

Patrick Stewart, who rose from poverty in England to become an accomplished Shakespearean stage actor and then achieved global stardom as the erudite Captain Jean-Luc Picard in TV’s Star Trek: The Next Generation and the telepathic Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men movies, has died at the age of 86.
Stewart, knighted in 2010 by Queen Elizabeth II for his contributions to drama, died at his home in Los Angeles, according to a statement on his X account.

“We announce with great sorrow the passing of Sir Patrick Stewart yesterday at his home in Los Angeles, in the loving care of his beloved wife Sunny, following a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s Disease and Lewy Body Dementia,” it said.

Stewart became an actor at age 18 and gained acclaim on the stage as a member of the Royal Shakespeare Company beginning in the 1960s. But it was not until after he was hired at age 47 for Star Trek: The Next Generation — a TV series that ran from 1987 to 1994 as a sequel to the original 1960s Star Trek — that he gained mainstream fame, acting into his 80s.
“Make it so,” his character Picard often said, instructing a subordinate to carry out a command, or sometimes deploying the similar catchphrase, “Engage.”

It was a role he had debated even taking after his longtime friend and fellow Shakespearean Ian McKellen advised him to spurn Star Trek and remain in theater. Stewart did take the role and became both a fan favorite and an indispensable part of a lucrative sci-fi franchise, playing Picard not only in 176 episodes over seven seasons of that series but also in several Star Trek films and in the later streaming series Star Trek: Picard that began airing in 2020 when he was 79.

“As the seven seasons of TNG (The Next Generation) went by, the distinction between Jean-Luc Picard and Patrick Stewart became thinner and thinner, until it was impossible for me to know where he left off and I began. So much of what I believed and felt went into that show,” Stewart told the Guardian newspaper in 2022.
Stewart also initially balked at being cast as the wheelchair-using mutant Professor X in the X-Men movies, based on the popular Marvel comic book character.

“I said, ‘Look, I know this isn’t science fiction, but it’s fantasy, and I’ve done that.’ But they persuaded me that it wouldn’t be like ‘Star Trek,’ so I did it. And yet again I was proved wrong,” Stewart told the Guardian.

He became a critical part of another big-money franchise, starting with the first entry X-Men in 2000 and followed by several more, including the 2002 Marvel movie Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness. He appeared alongside McKellen, who played the villain Magneto, in some of the X-Men films.

Stewart, playing Charles Xavier, took part in the filming of the highly anticipated Avengers: Doomsday and will appear in the Marvel film that is due to hit theaters in December. Marvel Studios paid tribute to Stewart on Thursday in a statement, calling him “a singular talent, a generous collaborator and a true gentleman.”

Stewart was born on July 13, 1940, in the English town of Mirfield in Yorkshire. He was raised in poverty, with a father who he said returned from World War Two an alcoholic who suffered from post-traumatic stress syndrome and physically abused Stewart’s mother. Stewart recalled putting his body between his father and mother to try to protect her.

As a child, Stewart said, acting became a “safe space” after a schoolteacher introduced him to Shakespeare — specifically The Merchant of Venice — during a class when he was 12. He started losing his hair at age 17 and was bald by 19. He was embarrassed at the time, but eventually embraced it.

Star Trek, created by Gene Roddenberry, presented a hopeful vision of the future, with humankind venturing into the cosmos in spaceships exceeding the speed of light and encountering alien races. The enduring popularity of the original series and the success of spinoff films prompted Roddenberry to create The Next Generation sequel series.

The Picard character was the opposite of the swashbuckling and sometimes unintentionally buffoonish Captain James T. Kirk, played by William Shatner, of the original series — envisioned as more cerebral and disciplined, though sometimes coming across as stuffy, humorless, or self-important.
Stewart recalled being a little bit too serious toward his cast mates early on.

“I tell the story of calling a meeting of my principal fellow cast members and telling them that I thought we were not disciplined enough, that we should not be fooling about on the set as much as we were but taking everything seriously,” Stewart told the New Yorker in 2023.

“And one of the cast members said, ‘Oh, come on, Patrick, we’ve got to have some fun.’ And I thumped the chair and said, ‘We are not here to have fun’ — which they have never let me forget. They taught me so much about loosening up and being freer,” Stewart added.
Stewart also felt the series improved as it went along, faulting his own portrayal of Picard in the first two seasons.
“I found it lacking intimacy. It was very authoritative, but there were few other qualities in him,” Stewart said, adding that his work got better in subsequent seasons.
In fact, the finest work for the entire cast may have been the two-part, time-bending series finale.

He became Sir Patrick Stewart when he was knighted by the queen at Buckingham Palace in 2010. He told reporters that his heroes were British actors Laurence Olivier, John Gielgud and Alec Guinness, who also had been knighted, adding that being “in that company is the grandest thing that has professionally happened to me.”

Great to be back at the #Emmys with @sunnyozell last night amongst so many actors, writers and directors whose work we’ve enjoyed watching over the past year. It’s been a while since a proper red carpet and I nearly forgot how to tie my bow tie. How’d I do? pic.twitter.com/VcLyEUxqOw— Patrick Stewart (@SirPatStew) September 20, 2021
Stewart was married three times and had two children. His third marriage, in 2013, was to American musician Sunny Ozell. – Rappler.com

articles.title: OpenAI asks B.C. court to quash privacy commissioner investigation of Tumbler Ridge shooting
articles.summary: OpenAI, the company behind the ChatGPT platform, is suing to quash an investigation launched in June by B.C.'s Office of the Information and Privacy Commissioner (OIPC) into the Tumbler Ridge…

image.caption: A man lays flowers at a memorial to the victims of the Tumbler Ridge Secondary School shooting in Tumbler Ridge, British Columbia, on Feb. 12, 2026. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

blocks.text: British Columbia

OpenAI, the company behind the ChatGPT platform, is suing to quash an investigation launched in June by B.C.'s Office of the Information and Privacy Commissioner (OIPC) into the Tumbler Ridge shooting.
Investigation strays beyond statutory and constitutional limits of OIPC's authority, says OpenAI
In a petition filed in B.C. Supreme Court, OpenAI says the investigation strays beyond the statutory and constitutional limits of the OIPC's authority.

"The OIPC has offered no coherent rationale for the investigation and, contrary to the Personal Information Protection Act (PIPA) … has identified no reasonable grounds to believe OpenAI breached that statute in connection with the Tumbler Ridge tragedy," reads the lawsuit.

Jesse Van Rootselaar, 18, died of a self-inflicted gunshot after killing six children and two adults on Feb. 10 in the small B.C. town. More than two dozen others were injured. Van Rootselaar allegedly used OpenAI's ChatGPT to help plan the massacre.

items: Accused Tumbler Ridge shooting co-conspirator enters not guilty plea in U.S. court

blocks.text: OpenAI has already said Van Rootselaar's activity was flagged internally for violent content and shut down.

Sam Altman, the CEO of OpenAI, wrote a letter of apology to the community of Tumbler Ridge for failing to notify authorities in Canada about the activity. The company later said it had failed to notice a second account created by Van Rootselaar after the first was disabled.
Eight people were killed in the Feb. 10, 2026, mass shooting in Tumbler Ridge. (CBC News)

In a statement published on Tuesday, one day after OpenAI filed the lawsuit, the OIPC said its investigation "is focused on whether the use of personal information (including as contained in and derived from prompts, uploaded content, usage data, interaction with other users) in the delivery of the service (i.e. ChatGPT responses) is one that a reasonable person would consider appropriate in the circumstances, including the potential for responses to influence behaviour."
The OIPC had not previously disclosed to the public it had opened an investigation into OpenAI.

items: Tumbler Ridge shooting survivor Maya Gebala being released from hospital, father says

blocks.text: OpenAI's lawsuit claims that even if the OIPC has reasonable grounds for an investigation, the issues have already been litigated in a three-year joint investigation by Canadian privacy regulators, including the OIPC.

That investigation concluded this past May, finding that Open AI lacked accountability and didn't follow Canadian law, and that it had launched ChatGPT without having fully addressed known privacy issues.

items: OpenAI didn't respect Canadian privacy law when it trained ChatGPT: investigation

blocks.text: OpenAI says commitments it has already made as a result of the national investigation would put it in compliance with PIPA, and that it should not have to face a "duplicative second investigation."
OpenAI also claims in its lawsuit that a "sweeping" production order issued by OIPC is "overbroad and unnecessary."

It says, among other things, the OIPC is demanding all of Van Rootselaar's chat logs, which have already been provided to law enforcement and the province, and all of OpenAI's records regarding its decision not to refer Van Rootselaar's account to law enforcement.

items: OpenAI asks California court to dismiss lawsuits over Tumbler Ridge shooting

blocks.text: In September, the B.C. government announced it is suing OpenAI in its home base of California based on the company's failure to notify police of threats made on ChatGPT before the mass shooting.
The company and CEO Altman are also facing dozens of civil suits filed on behalf of victims, survivors and witnesses.

The OIPC has jurisdiction over organizations that collect, use and disclose the personal information of people living in British Columbia. To conduct those activities, an organization must have legal authorization, the office said in its statement.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Karin Larsen is a former Olympian and award-winning sports broadcaster who covers news and sports for CBC Vancouver.

articles.title: Manosphere and online misogyny should be treated as public health issues, say UK experts
articles.summary:
Report calls for an effort to tackle harms in similar way to obesity and smoking, and stresses need to ‘offer boys something better’

The manosphere and online misogyny should be treated by…
articles.byline: Tobi Thomas Health and inequalities correspondent

blocks.text: The manosphere and online misogyny should be treated by the government as a public health issue, in the same way as obesity or smoking, experts have said.

Writing in the Lancet, the authors of a new report argue that a coordinated response is needed, involving governments, schools, health services and community organisations, similar to the public-health response to tobacco use and ultra-processed food.

“Men’s problems are framed [in the manosphere] as the result of feminism rather than structural conditions, and masculine identity is commodified through products and paid content that normalise and reinforce health-harming and performance-oriented masculinities,” the authors write.
The report defines the manosphere as “a diffuse commercial ecosystem and loose collection of online communities united by shared beliefs about masculinity, misogyny and male victimisation”.
It goes on to outline how the manosphere has evolved into a highly lucrative online industry that makes money by promoting “the most extreme expressions of misogyny and aggrieved masculinity”.

Prof Kent Buse, a co-author of the paper and co-founder of the social justice thinktank Global 50/50, said: “This is a business model, not a fringe. Outrage and grievance are good for business, so the system rewards the most extreme content. Expect the playbook that served tobacco so well: blame the individual, and call regulation an attack on freedom. Public health has a tested toolkit for commercial harms and we should use it.”
He added: “Boys and men are not the problem. The problem is the conditions that leave them isolated and without a secure future, and the companies that profit from their anger and insecurity.”
after newsletter promotion

The authors also point to growing disengagement from education among boys around the world, as well as loneliness, money worries and social exclusion, which can leave young men searching for a sense of belonging. These problems, they say, can make them more vulnerable to online communities that offer simple explanations for their difficulties and often encourage them to blame women and feminism.
Prof Sarah Hawkes, the report’s other author, said: “The manosphere offers boys and young men belonging, identity and an explanation for why life feels hard.

“Those needs are real. A response that only removes the manosphere, without offering something credible in its place, will fail. We need to offer boys something better, not just tell them what to avoid.”

Mark Brooks, the policy and communications director at the Centre for Policy Research on Men and Boys, welcomed the report’s position that it was a public health issue and that men, boys, women and girls were all victims of this content.

“Far too often, the manosphere discussion has positioned all men and boys as a problem and not taken into account the broader economic, educational and cultural challenges that drive their engagement,” he said.
“Not all men and boys engage with this content equally. We are currently working on research to identify who is most at risk.”

articles.title: FACT CHECK: Jinggoy Estrada not acquitted of plunder; bail hearing ongoing
articles.summary: For non-bailable cases like plunder, a petition for bail needs to be filed. The court then holds summary hearings to determine whether the evidence of guilt is strong.

blocks.text: Claim: Senator Jinggoy Estrada is acquitted of plunder.
Why we fact-checked this: The YouTube post containing the claim has over 12,563 views as of writing.
The post, dated October 24, is titled, “SAWAKAS! GOODNEWS TO! KAPAPASOK LANG! SEN J1NGG0Y ESTRADA PANALO sa PANGYAYARING TO B0Y1NG NA1SAHAN?”
(Finally! This is good news! Just in! Senator Jinggoy Estrada outsmarts Boying and wins case!)
The video also has a thumbnail that says, “Abswelto na! Lalaya na! Mga kaso! Binasura na!”
(Acquitted and is now free! Cases are junked!)
The facts: Estrada is still incarcerated at the New Quezon City Jail following his arrest over plunder, bribery, and graft cases related to Bulacan flood control projects. Plunder is non-bailable.

The senator has an ongoing bail hearing at the Sandiganbayan Fifth Division for his plunder, contrary to the claim that said the anti-graft court already acquitted Estrada. If the court finds that the evidence is weak, it will grant the bail petition. (READ: Revilla’s P1-M bail: What ‘weak evidence’ bought him)

Flood control corruption: The Office of the Ombudsman ordered Estrada’s arrest on June 1, over allegations pointing to the senator receiving over P573 million in kickbacks from public infrastructure projects.

Aside from Estrada, the Ombudsman also filed charges against former Department of Public Works and Highways Secretary Manuel Bonoan and other key DPWH officials over their involvement in flood control-related budget insertions. On June 30, the Ombudsman turned Bonoan into a state witness, leaving Estrada the sole defendant in the case involving alleged misuse of public works funds.
On October 27, 2026, Bonoan appeared at Estrada’s bail hearing and testified that the senator had at least P7.4 billion in congressional initiatives in 2025.
Previous related fact-checks: Rappler has previously debunked several claims surrounding the multi-billion-peso Philippine flood control scandal.

articles.title: Polymarket temporarily suspends trading on international platform due to security incident
articles.summary:
Security incident linked to performance-monitoring tool spurred platform to halt trading for about an hour

Polymarket temporarily halted trading on its international platform on Thursday…

blocks.text: Polymarket temporarily halted trading on its international platform on Thursday because of a security incident that compromised a third-party provider, the company said.
Trading was paused for about an hour and resumed on Thursday afternoon. The company has promised to fully reimburse any affected traders.
The prediction market platform said it halted trading “out of an abundance of caution” after identifying and fixing the issue affecting its international platform.
“We’ll make this right and are fully reimbursing all affected traders,” the company posted on X once trading had resumed.
Polymarket said it referred the incident to a law enforcement agency in the United Kingdom.
Reports have linked the source of the incident to DebugBear, a UK-based company offering website performance-monitoring tools.

DebugBear’s own website was unavailable on Thursday afternoon and the company posted on X that it was “impacted by an ongoing security incident”. It also advised clients who were using one of its products to remove the embed code from their websites. The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

It was not immediately clear to what extent traders using the popular prediction market platform were affected, or the breadth of the impact. The company said anyone who was affected “will be made whole”.

articles.title: 70% of eligible voters turned out for Alberta referendum question on separation
articles.summary: Alberta's referendum question on separation drew more interest from voters than the province's last general election, according to the official results released Thursday.

image.caption: The official results of the Alberta referendum have been released, 10 days after the vote was held. The official numbers vary by less than a percentage point from those originally posted. (Zazak Bouarab/Radio-Canada)

blocks.text: Calgary·New
Alberta's referendum question on separation drew more interest from voters than the province's last general election, according to the official results released Thursday.
Turnout for separation question 10 percentage points higher than the last provincial election
The final tally of the referendum ballots has been released, 10 days after the vote was held.
More than 2.2 million ballots were cast for the separation question, representing a 70.4 per cent voter turnout — nearly 10 percentage points higher than for the 2023 provincial election.

Albertans soundly rejected the proposal to hold a second, binding referendum on separation, with 74.9 per cent voting against, while narrowly passing the five immigration questions and voting down the four constitutional questions.
Mapping out where Albertans voted to remain (or not) in Canada

A total of 22.1 million votes were cast across the 10 questions, including declined and rejected ballots. The turnout on all questions was around 70 per cent. (Voters could choose which questions they wanted to vote on.)

items: Smith scores slim majority on immigration questions, Albertans reject constitutional changes
Nopes to the nine? Blue walls? Five takeaways from Alberta's referendum results

blocks.text: The turnout for the other nine questions came as a surprise to Mount Royal University political scientist Lori Williams.
"I think there was a sense that maybe there might be a big gap between the separation question participation rate and the responses on the other nine questions," Williams said.

"Even though those questions were complex, those who did show up and didn't leave the lineup, who went through the trouble to actually do the mail-in or the advance polls or the referendum day voting, almost all of them went through those questions."
But with that high turnout came slim majorities for the five questions that passed.
The immigration questions passed with between 51.7 and 58 per cent support. Williams says those results are "not a really strong mandate" for Premier Danielle Smith.
"It didn't give the government the authority to sort of take the fight to Ottawa in the way that they had hoped to do," Williams said.
Mount Royal University political scientist Lori Williams on Oct. 29, 2026. (Chelsey Mutter/CBC)
The remaining four questions on constitutional reform failed, with between 42.4 and 47.2 per cent voting in favour.

Williams said internal polling and focus groups had led the province to expect a much higher success rate on the questions, and the province "might be more reluctant to go forward with a referendum" in the future since the results turned out so differently than expected.
"That's got to be a bit of a cautionary note," she said.

items: Edmonton and Calgary rejected her referendum. Does Danielle Smith have a city problem?
Alberta pursuing own dental, drug plans despite referendum defeat on federal opt-outs

blocks.text: Elections Alberta to review how referendum went
The official numbers vary by less than a percentage point from the unofficial results available since Sunday.
Counting all of those ballots by hand took about five days, with unofficial results finalized well beyond the 48-hour deadline set out in Alberta's referendum legislation.
Why are votes being counted by hand?

An Elections Alberta spokesperson told CBC News the provincial agency is not yet ready to discuss lessons learned from the tumultuous process, and that it "will be conducting reviews, debriefs, data analysis, and data entry" over the next few months.

items: Q&A: Elections Alberta explains why the referendum took so long to count

blocks.text: The agency said the referendum had the highest number of ballots to count by hand in any Canadian electoral event, to its knowledge.

articles.title: Germany's Alexander Zverev clinches tennis No. 1 ranking
articles.summary: Alexander Zverev is the second German man, after Boris Becker, to clinch the No. 1 spot in tennis.

image.caption: A German male tennis player had not reached No. 1 in 35 yearsImage: Achmad Ibrahim/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: German tennis star Alexander Zverev is set to become the new world No. 1 in tennis, capping a successful year where he won two Grand Slams.
Zverev is the second German man, after Boris Becker, to clinch the top spot in the sport. Becker reached No.1 some 35 years ago.
Zverev replaces Italy's Jannik Sinner, who previously held the world's No. 1 spot.
Zverev got there by reaching the quarter-finals of the Erste Bank Open in Vienna this week.
He is also the second-oldest first-time No. 1 ranked player after Australian John Newcombe.
"(It is) very special. To have the feeling to be on the top of the world is amazing," Zverev said.
"It is different than winning a tournament or a title, but it's such a special feeling to know that the No. 1 is going to be next to your name when the new rankings come out."
Among German female tennis players, only Steffi Graf and Angelique Kerber have achieved this in the WTA rankings.

blocks.caption: Zverev beat Ben Shelton to win the US Open in SeptemberImage: Robert Deutsch/IMAGN Images/REUTERS

blocks.text: Two Grand Slams in 2026
Zverev's career had been defined by getting close to Grand Slam titles but never quite reaching them, facing stiff competition from Sinner and Spanish talent Carlos Alcaraz.
The Hamburg-born also won a gold medal in the 2021 Olympics.
But his tennis career finally had its breakthrough this year, when he won the Grand Slam at both the French and US Opens.
Known for his consistency, he was just the ninth man to reach at least the semifinals at all four majors in the same season.

articles.title: 'Star Trek' star Patrick Stewart dies age 86
articles.summary: The Shakespearean actor landed the role of a lifetime as "Star Trek" Captain Picard. He passed away at age 86.

image.caption: Stewart needed his agent's encouragement to take on the role of Captain Jean-Luc PicardImage: Willy Sanjuan/picture alliance

blocks.text: For Star Trek fans, he was the legendary Captain Picard; the British actor and director Patrick Stewart, longtime member of the Royal Shakespeare Company, died on Thursday at the age of 86 following a "brief and poignant journey" with Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body dementia, according to an official statement on his social media accounts.

In Los Angeles, California, far away from the small English village of Mirfield where he was born, Stewart achieved world fame. He was 47 years old when he landed the role of a lifetime in the legendary science fiction series Star Trek: Playing Captain Jean-Luc Picard in "Star Trek: The Next Generation," he stepped into the shoes of the legendary Captain James T. Kirk, played by William Shatner.

Stewart brought a calm, measured and distinctly British presence that quickly made Picard a fan favorite and a cult figure in the Star Trek universe. He returned to the role decades later in the spin-off series "Star Trek: Picard," which ended in 2023, proving the character's enduring appeal.

As Captain Jean-Luc Picard, he led the crew of the starship Enterprise, a spaceship with the sizeable mission: "To explore strange new worlds. To seek out new life and new civilizations" — and most importantly, "to boldly go where no man has gone before!"

blocks.caption: In addition to Star Trek, Stewart also had a leading role in the X-Men franchiseImage: dpa-Film Fox/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: In love with Shakespeare
Stewart's interest in acting was sparked in the early 1950s when a teacher asked him to recite a work by Shakespeare. His passion for Shakespeare stayed with him until the end.

His parents were far removed from the glamor of the theatrical world. His father was a highly respected officer in the British Army during World War II, but at home, he was an abusive husband, and young Patrick had to helplessly witness repeated violence against his mother. Stewart wrote about his experiences with domestic violence in The Guardian in 2009. The stage, he confessed there, seemed to him "a far safer place" than reality; he saw acting as a way to escape his home life.

Patrick began acting at the age of 12. At 16, he left school early and, thanks to a scholarship, studied acting in Bristol, England. Along the way, he worked as a journalist. In 1965, he became an official member of the Royal Shakespeare Company, and remained with the theather company from 1966 to 1982. Such was his passion for the great English playwright and lyricist that he even shared his sonnets on his Twitter account during the 2020 coronavirus pandemic.

Stewart dazzled the theater world with his own stage adaptation of Charles Dickens' 1843 tale "A Christmas Carol." He played more than 30 roles himself. After its 1987 premiere in Stewart's hometown of Mirfield, the one-man show became a critics' favorite and a long-running hit on Broadway in New York.
'Star Trek' offer from Hollywood

In the same year, Stewart went from being a stage actor to an international TV star. Star Trek producer Robert Justman offered him the role of Captain Jean-Luc Picard, one of the main characters in a new edition of the popular TV series "Star Trek: The Next Generation."

The successful Shakespearean hesitated. Until then, he had never worked in Hollywood. But his agent encouraged him to accept the role, Stewart recalled in a 2020 interview with the German newspaper Die Welt. "You can accept the offer as a start for now. It won't be a big deal, you can't revive a series as iconic as Star Trek anyway."

blocks.caption: EngageImage: Paramount/Courtesy Everett Collection/picture alliance

blocks.text: Adventures in the universe

But his agent was to be proven wrong: Stewart led the Starship Enterprise through its galactic adventures for seven seasons and four full-length feature films. The TV series had astronomical success on Earth in a very short time.

At first, the producers were at odds as to whether Stewart's British accent could really fit the role of commander of a US starship in the 24th century, but it soon became impossible to imagine the series without the subtly diplomatic Captain Picard, who often quoted Shakespeare while at the helm. It seemed as if all the time he had spent as a Shakespearean actor had prepared him to command the Enterprise, Stewart once remarked with a wink. When the cult series ended in 1994, he had ruled out ever returning to the Enterprise's command center.
In 2010, the actor was knighted by the Queen of England. Stewart considered it the greatest honor of his career to stand alongside acting greats such as Sir Laurence Olivier and Sir Alec Guinness.

Beyond the screen, Stewart has long used his voice for social and human rights causes. In recent years, he has drawn attention to issues such as violence against women, age discrimination and the protection of children.

blocks.caption: Stewart was a vocal and engaged civil rights activistImage: epa PA West/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: A short-lived retirement

In a June 2020 interview, "Playboy" asked the New York resident whether he was considering retiring from acting. "Never! That would mean giving up my life," replied Stewart, who was approaching his 80th birthday at the time. He was filming the second of three seasons of "Star Trek: Picard." The series ends with a final episode in which the retired Starfleet admiral makes his last appearance. In the series, Picard retires to his family vineyard in France but is drawn back into space to confront new threats to the Federation.

blocks.caption: Stewart returned to Star Trek for the series "Star Trek: Picard"Image: Matt Kennedy/CBS/Amazon/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: This series also showcases Stewart's affection for his pit bull, Ginger. In "Star Trek: Picard," Picard also has a pit bull, a loyal four-legged companion named Number One — a deliberate reference to Stewart's real-life love of the breed. For his efforts to combat prejudice against pit bulls and to support their adoption, Stewart was honored by the US animal welfare organization ASPCA, among others.
In 2024, he published his memoir "Making it So." In it, he recounts his passion for theater and his love of Shakespeare.
Now, at the age of 86, the British actor has finally departed for another galaxy. Farewell, Patrick Stewart!
Translated from German by Sarah Hucal.

articles.title: Hegseth reportedly fires high-ranking army strategist over alleged leaks
articles.summary:
Pentagon says it has referred leak case to justice department for criminal investigation

The US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, has reportedly dismissed Lt Gen Brett Sylvia, a high-ranking…

blocks.text: The US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, has reportedly dismissed Lt Gen Brett Sylvia, a high-ranking army strategist serving on the Pentagon’s joint staff, following allegations that he disclosed classified information to the public.

The Pentagon announced on Thursday that it had referred an alleged information leak case for criminal investigation, maintaining that the removal of the senior general was essential “to protect sensitive information”, the Washington Post reported.
Sylvia had served as the director for strategy, plans and policy on the joint staff.
Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell acknowledged the dismissal in a statement on social media, though he did not mention Sylvia by name.

“Following an extensive Air Force OSI investigation, the Department took necessary personnel action to protect sensitive information,” Parnell wrote. “To protect the integrity of the investigation, no further comment will be made regarding the individual or the circumstances of this action.”
“This matter, along with others, have been referred to the Justice Department for potential further legal action,” he added.

Sylvia’s removal represents one of the most significant actions so far in Hegseth’s extensive campaign to identify officials suspected of sharing information with journalists, as the unpopular US war on Iran moves into its ninth month.

In July, Hegseth ​announced that the Pentagon and the US Department of Justice had created a joint taskforce “​to identify and ​prosecute” what he called the “unauthorized disclosure ​of sensitive” information to the press.
Last year, Hegseth implemented new restrictions governing media access that prompted legal concerns from press organizations.
Dozens of journalists surrendered their press badges rather than agree to the new media policies, which have been subject to legal challenges.
A senior Pentagon official told Reuters that Sylvia failed three separate polygraph tests, in which he was asked whether he had disclosed classified material.

“The extent of his leaking became so critical that Secretary Hegseth took immediate action and fired Sylvia in order to protect national security. Urgent action was needed and could not wait another second,” the official said, according to Reuters.

However, a colleague of Sylvia told the Washington Post that the general had consistently rejected accusations that he leaked classified information, while also acknowledging that he had previously communicated with members of the press.

In August, three journalists fired by the Pentagon from the US government-funded news outlet Stars and Stripes sued the department in federal court, arguing their dismissals were illegal and violated their first amendment rights to free speech.

articles.title: Ottawa's sluggish bureaucracy leaves critical gaps in Canadian military ammo supply: AG
articles.summary: A new audit reveals Canada's strategic ammunition stockpile cannot support war readiness or NATO commitments. The report blames Public Services and Procurement Canada for slow restocking, alongside…

image.caption: A new audit reveals Canada's strategic ammunition stockpile cannot support war readiness or NATO commitments. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

A new audit reveals Canada's strategic ammunition stockpile cannot support war readiness or NATO commitments. The report blames Public Services and Procurement Canada for slow restocking, alongside National Defence for failing to manage regular inventory. Despite a $9.2-billion funding pledge, fixing these critical capability gaps will take several years.
Auditor general slams defence, procurement departments over shortage

A new report by the auditor general takes shots at both the Department of National Defence and Public Services and Procurement Canada over their handling of the Canadian military's strategic stockpile of ammunition.

Karen Hogan's latest report, tabled on Thursday, concluded that the Defence Department does not manage its ammunition to meet its regular use and strategic stockpile needs and the federal procurement agency was slow in efforts to restock ammunition.
Her analysis found that the strategic stockpile, which the military needs in case of war, did not contain "all the types and quantities of ammunition required" and there were significant gaps.
More importantly, perhaps, Hogan noted that the problem is affecting Canada's international commitments.
Auditor general says Canada's military stockpile has 'critical gaps'

"As at March 2026, National Defence determined that the Canadian Armed Forces' readiness level to meet North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) commitments was well below target, and ammunition was one of the contributing capability shortfalls, especially for the strategic stockpile," said the audit.

The scathing assessment was released on the same day federal officials released the country's new national security strategy, which warned Canada needed to "prepare for all contingencies up to and including war."

The auditor's report noted that in 2024, the federal government dedicated $9.2 billion over 13 years to support strategic stockpile replenishment, and some contracts have been awarded. But at the current pace, it will take several years to close the gaps.
When it comes to buying ammunition, the auditor looked at 15 regular‑use ammunition contracts and found it took an average of almost 19 months from contract signature to final delivery.
In addition, Public Services and Procurement Canada "did not consistently track and document why contracts were changed to extend delivery dates."

items: Canada's new national security strategy will shield economy, modernize military

blocks.text: The audit also pointed out how the military — when it had ammunition — only used about half of what was allocated.
Hogan suggested that "limited or cancelled" training activities were likely to blame, but the Defence Department did not track or explain the reasons.

"For example, National Defence's analysis as at March 2026 noted that equipment, such as tanks and ships, was often out of service, which limited their availability for use in training and military exercises," said the audit.
"Other factors, such as a lack of personnel or poor environmental conditions, might have also prevented these activities."
Defence minister embraces recommendations
Defence Minister David McGuinty said increasing the military's supply of ammunition is among the government's top defence priorities.
"The entire auditor general report on ammunition tells us that we have progress to make, and we're making it," McGuinty told reporters after the report was tabled.
"We accept and embrace all of those recommendations. In fact, we're acting on most of them already."
Canada's former top military commander sounded the alarm three years ago about the critical state of the military's ammunition supply.
The report says the munitions shortfall will take years to resolve. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)
Retired general Wayne Eyre, the former chief of the defence staff, also criticized lack of industrial capacity for military ammunition.

Appearing before a House of Commons committee, he warned that if the Canadian military consumed ammunition at the same rate as seen in the war in Ukraine, Canada would exhaust much of its ammunition stock within days.
Eyre also pointed out that — at the time — no new production lines had been opened to address the shortage.

He said that when Canada started providing military aid to Ukraine, it did so from "pretty empty" shelves, noting that domestic industrial capacity to regenerate artillery pieces, rockets and ammunition was largely non-existent.

items: Canada, Ukraine forge 100-year pact built on drones and defence

blocks.text: The Conservative Opposition said the situation is critical and cannot be allowed to continue.

"The Liberals must act immediately to rectify the unacceptable state of Canada's ammunition stockpiles: both inventory and accounting," said defence critic James Bezan. "This is not an insurmountable problem. It is a question of political will."
In addition to the money committed in 2024, the federal government in March of this year released a $1.4-billion framework to rapidly scale up domestic munitions production.
The plan includes a $305-million investment IMT Precision, in Ingersoll, Ont., and nearly $1 billion to General Dynamics Ordnance and Tactical Systems in Quebec for artillery round production.
Among other things, there are also plans to construct a domestic nitrocellulose production facility, which critically supports the supply of ammunition.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Murray Brewster is the senior defence writer for CBC News, based in Ottawa. He has covered the Canadian military and foreign policy from Parliament Hill for over a decade. Among other assignments, he spent a total of 15 months on the ground covering the Afghan war for The Canadian Press. Prior to that, he covered defence issues and politics for CP in Nova Scotia for 11 years and was bureau chief for Standard Broadcast News in Ottawa.
