articles.title: Young athlete and former minister among victims of Spain train crash
articles.summary: As some of the victims' names are released publicly, an outpouring of grief and anger is sweeping across Spain.

blocks.text: Image source, RFEA
Julieta Gallego, a long-jump athlete, was a regular on Spain's athletics circuit
ByAlicia Curry and Tiffany Wertheimer
A 24-year-old athlete and a former government minister are among the victims of a deadly train crash that killed 69 people near Urda in central Spain on Wednesday morning.
The crash, between a high-speed Renfe train and a stationary Iryo train on the same track, also injured more than 100 people injured, many seriously.
The impact caused carriages to derail, and there are fears the death toll could still rise, with reports of family members searching for missing relatives in hospitals across the region.
The bodies of those killed have been taken to the main forensics institute in Toledo, where families have been giving DNA samples to help identify them.
The crash is the second rail disaster in Spain this year, and the worst in the country's history since 2013.
Who are the victims?
Julieta Gallego
Julieta Gallego, 24, was a Spanish long jumper who competed for Madrid athletics club, AD Sprint.
"The entire club is heartbroken," it wrote on Instagram.
The Royal Spanish Athletics Federation (RFEF) announced her death, external, expressing its condolences to her family, friends and teammates.
Gallego regularly competed in Spanish club championships, local media outlet ABC reported, external, and had a best jump of 5.9m (19ft 3in).
Raúl Chapado, president of RFEF, told the outlet that her death is a "blow that strikes at the very heart of the athletics family."
"Today, the sport mourns the passing of Julieta, a life ahead of her that has been unjustly extinguished".

blocks.caption: Image caption, Fátima Báñez, pictured in 2025

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
Fátima Báñez, pictured in 2025
Fátima Báñez
The death of former employment minister Fátima Báñez, 59, was confirmed by the Spanish Confederation of Business Organizations (CEOE), which she chaired.
"Her warmth, generosity, and commitment leave an indelible mark on businesses and the entire CEOE team," it said in a statement.

Báñez served in the government under former Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy from 2011 until 2018, and was the first woman to hold the role. In 2012, she introduced controversial labour reforms that made it easier for companies to fire people, sparking mass protests across the country.
Following news of her death, Madrid regional president Isabel Díaz Ayuso paid tribute to her, saying she would be "deeply missed".
"Spain loses a great political figure," she said.
Watch: What leaked audio reveals about Spain train crash
José Manuel Chacón
The Civil Guard confirmed the death, external of its officer José Manuel Chacón, 31, in a statement expressing its "deepest condolences" to his family, friends and colleagues.
Antonio Montero Domínguez
Finance and tax lawyer, Antonio Montero Domínguez, was remembered as a "meticulous professional" and "tireless worker" by legal news website, El Derecho, external.
His death was confirmed by Spain's tax authority, external, where he had been an inspector between 2012-2016.
Additional reporting by Sarah Rainsford, Madeleine Lake, and Tom McArthur

articles.title: Justice for Maya women in Guatemala, girls back in school in India, restored land in Mali: The UN has named its 2026 SDG Action Award winners
articles.summary: Champions of indigenous women's rights in Guatemala, girls' education in India, and restored farmland in Mali all featured among the winners of UN's SDG Action Awards.

image.caption: Rokiatou Traore received the Changemaker AwardImage: UN SDG Action Campaign/Sabrina Marchionne

blocks.text: A legal aid group for Indigenous women in Guatemala, a movement of village mothers in rural India, and a Malian entrepreneur who restores farmland have won this year's UN SDG Action Awards.
The winners were announced at the ninth Heroes of Tomorrow awards ceremony in Rome, Italy, run by the UN SDG Action Campaign. They were chosen from more than 7,000 entries from 190 countries.
Nine finalists were shortlisted for three categories: resilience, creativity and changemaker.

The Resilience Award went to the Women's Justice Initiative. Many indigenous women in Guatemala face high rates of violence, poverty and discrimination, made worse by language barriers and a lack of access to information. The initiative helps women and girls get access to justice and lead change in their communities. According to the organization, more than 16,000 women and girls have participated.

"I accept the UN SDG Action Award in the honour of the Maya Kaqchikel women and girls in Guatemala who are building a more just future for their communities. Ending violence against women requires all of us. Only together, we can build a future where every woman and girl lives with dignity and realizes her full potential," said Viviana Patal, the initiative's legal director.

blocks.caption: Jannat Al Ghezi (second from left) paid an emotional tribute to campaigner Yanar MohammedImage: UN SDG Action Campaign/Sabrina Marchionne

blocks.text: Keeping girls in school in India

The Creativity Award was given to Mothers of Courage, a grassroots campaign that aims to keep girls in education in rural India. Its organizers say more than 1.2 million people have joined and pledged to keep their daughters in education and to prevent early marriage.

"This award today belongs to all the mothers in those villages, all the women leaders, who are working hard to change the destinies of their daughters and their daughters-in-law," said Khushboo Awasthi, Mothers of Courage's chief curator.
"Together, let's create a world where no girl ever has to negotiate for her right to dream and to aspire and to thrive."
Trees and livelihoods in Mali

The Changemaker Award when to Malian entrepreneur Rokiatou Traore. Her organization, Herou Alliance, helps women and small farmers bring worn-out land back to life by planting trees alongside their crops. The trees also help farmers generate extra revenue, allowing them to sell products from moringa and other valuable trees.

"Receiving this award means a lot to me. It is a reminder of why I started this journey," said Traore. "I invite you all to join us, to plant more trees, to empower more women, and above all, to create a future full of opportunities for communities for today and for future generations."

The UN Trust Fund to End Violence against Women and Girls received an honorable mention. Speaking about the award, President of the Organization of Women's Freedom in Iraq Jannat Al Ghezi paid a tearful tribute to its founder Yanar Mohammed, who was assassinated outside her home in Baghdad in March.
'Be that change'

UN Assistant Secretary-General Michelle Muschett said the finalists "remind us that the future is something we create together and that each of us has the power to help shape it and open doors for the next generations."

"When they tell you that one person cannot make a difference, prove them wrong," UN SDG Action Campaign Director Marina Ponti told the audience. "Change has always begun with people who refused to accept that the world could not be different. So be courageous. Be persistent. Be that change."

blocks.caption: Italian singer-songwriter Roshelle performed at the ceremonyImage: UN SDG Action Campaign/Sabrina Marchionne

blocks.text: How are the awards organized?

A panel of 20 judges from UN leadership, government, civil society, the arts, business and youth activism chose the winners. They included UN Development Programme Administrator Alexander De Croo, Oxfam International Executive Director Amitabh Behar, and Otto Group Vice President Tobias Wollermann.

The awards are run by the UN SDG Action Campaign, a special initiative of the UN Secretary-General. The campaign supports the UN Sustainable Development Goals, 17 targets adopted by member states that cover areas including poverty, hunger, education, gender equality and climate protection.
The awards are supported by Italy's Foreign Ministry and Germany's Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development.
Editor's Note: DW Director General Barbara Massing was a member of the 20-person jury panel.

articles.title: B.C. NDP caucus taps Jennifer Whiteside to be new interim leader
articles.summary: The B.C. NDP has announced Jennifer Whiteside as its new interim leader.

image.caption: Jennifer Whiteside, MLA-elect for New Westminster-Coquitlam, has been named interim NDP leader after a caucus meeting Thursday. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

blocks.text: British Columbia
The B.C. NDP has announced Jennifer Whiteside as its new interim leader.
David Eby stepped down as leader after Saturday's election loss
The B.C. NDP caucus has announced Jennifer Whiteside as its choice for the party's new interim leader.
The caucus recommended Whiteside after David Eby resigned as party leader when his snap election call resulted in a resounding defeat of the NDP at the polls.
Eby's majority government fell from 47 seats in the legislature to 28, according to the initial count.
At a caucus meeting Thursday, Mike Farnworth was named house leader and Niki Sharma was named caucus chair.

items: Wounded B.C. NDP caucus meets after humbling election defeat
5 reasons why Lorne Doerkson is the next premier of British Columbia

blocks.text: Whiteside said it was a unanimous recommendation.
Eby wasn't at the in-person caucus meeting, nor was he present virtually, Whiteside said.
Whiteside said she was humbled by the caucus's recommendation.
"It is not an outcome I was necessarily expecting," she said.
She said she's looking forward to using her advocacy skills in the role.
Whiteside, MLA-elect for New Westminster-Coquitlam, previously worked as chief spokesperson and lead negotiator for the Hospital Employees' Union.
She said the caucus meeting included discussions on what the community needs.
"We are very focused on making sure that British Columbians understand that we are standing for them, that we have their backs, and we will continue to do that work in the opposition caucus."
The B.C. NDP will serve as Official Opposition to Lorne Doerkson's B.C. Conservative Party, which won 63 seats.
More to come.
With files from Katie DeRosa and Lauren Vanderdeen

articles.title: Berlin's Elif Eralp under fire over Der Spiegel interview
articles.summary: Left candidate Elif Eralp has sparked controversy after Der Speigel reported she was advised against mentioning a pro-Palestinian activist for fear of reprisals against her family.

image.caption: Left candidate Elif Eralp has made clear she'll be tough on crime in comments later in the dayImage: Fabian Sommer/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Elif Eralp, the candidate on course to become the next mayor of Berlin, sparked controversy on Thursday after having unintentionally aired personal security fears that appeared to be linked to pro-Palestinian activists in the city.
The controversy came about based on internal remarks that were part of her interview with the German news magazine Der Spiegel.

Eralp, whose Left Party (Die Linke) came out on top in local elections in Berlin last month, appeared to suggest in remarks made during an internal authorization process for an interview that she gave to Der Spiegel that she couldn't make references to a particular pro-Palestinian activist out of fear for her own safety.
"I can't put myself and my family in danger for Der Spiegel," the magazine cites her as having written in a Word Document edit, which was inadvertently sent back to the reporters.

"What do we do now? Cancel the whole interview?" she is cited as having asked her press officer and other party colleagues, while stating in another remark, "I should never have agreed to this interview."
Elif Eralp under pressure to clearly label out threats she sees

In the Der Spiegel interview, which was conducted on Monday in Eralp's office in Berlin's House of Representatives, the 45-year-old was asked about allegations of antisemitism that have been leveled at members of her socialist party.
Those accusations came about after at least two instances where people with questionable backgrounds showed up to celebrate after Eralp's party won elections in the city state last month.

For instance, the Left Party election celebration in the Berlin district of Neukölln was attended by a controversial pro-Palestinian activist associated with the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PFLP), which is classified as a terrorist organization by the European Union.

In the past, Ibrahim Ibrahim has described Yahya Sinwar, the former head of Hamas in Gaza, widely regarded as the mastermind behind the deadly terror attack on Israel on October 7, 2023, as a "martyr" and a "hero." He has since rejected accusations of antisemitism and of supporting terrorism or Hamas.

Asked by Der Spiegel whether she was referring to the Ibrahim incident, Eralp initially responded with a "yes." But she later returned the interview transcript to the magazine with the question crossed out and the comment regarding her and her family's safety.
In Germany, it is standard practice for an interviewee to review and approve direct quotations with media outlets before the interview is published.

In notes included in the approved version of the transcript, which Der Spiegel believes were left in by accident, Eralp wrote that Berlin police had previously advised her not to comment on specific individuals.
Der Spiegel on why it published the notes
That Eralp chose to conceal her concerns publicly led some politicians to ask whether she was the right person to be the mayor of Berlin.
Der Spiegel wrote in its story:

"There were reasons not to publish – Eralp's security concerns first and foremost," the magazine wrote. "But the political importance of her notes outweighed them. Der Spiegel believes that the public should know."
It added that the story begs the question: "Can a woman who is too scared to name a terrorist sympathizer in an interview be responsible for the security of all Berliners?"
SPD, Greens also weigh in
Rival politicians weighed in, including from the Social Democrats (SPD) and Greens, with whom the Left Party is due to conduct coalition talks in Berlin next month.
"I would advise my party to distance itself from an alliance with the Left Party," said the SPD's Karl Lauterbach, who rose to prominence as Germany's health minister during the Covid-19 pandemic.
"Further talks about a coalition with this party should be out of the question for any social democrat," added SPD internal affairs spokesman Sebastian Fiedler.

Katharina Dröge, the leader of the Green Party's parliamentary grouping, asked in the Süddeutsche Zeitung newspaper, "Will [Eralp] continue to let herself be influenced by those in her own ranks who are close to criminal groups and who tolerate threats and intimidation towards their own lead candidate? Or will she manage to give a clear and tough response?"

The chairman of the Central Council of Jews in Germany, Josef Schuster, warned: "The SPD and the Greens have a duty not to hand governmental responsibility for Berlin and for the security of the Jewish community to the Left Party" and claimed the story showed that "the Left Party is incapable of distancing itself from terrorist sympathizers and antisemites."
Eralp issues tough response, hits out at critics

Eralp hit back later on Thursday, slamming a "truly toxic debate," vowing not to be intimidated and promising a tough stance "against organized crime, against organizations that glorify violence, against violence, against terror."
She said she wouldn't comment on the specifics of the Der Spiegel story but insisted that she would "ensure the security of all Berliners."
Eralp also received backing from the vice-president of the German parliament and veteran Left Party colleague Bodo Ramelow, who criticized the Der Spiegel story as "more than questionable."

He said the reporting "targeted a person who feels vulnerable and made them even more vulnerable." He said internal communications had been used to depict the "anachronistic cliché" of a "weak woman."

articles.title: Watch: What leaked audio reveals about Spain train crash
articles.summary: Recordings between a control centre and the train drivers appear to show one train was given clearance to move even though another train had stalled on the track.

blocks.text: Leaked audio recordings published by Spanish media have shed light on communications between a control centre and train drivers in the moments before two trains collided outside Toledo.
Officials are investigating the cause of the disaster, which occurred when a train from Madrid to Seville barrelled into a stationary train.
Southern Europe correspondent Sarah Rainsford explains what the audio reveals.

articles.title: DHS cites risk to more than 40,000 personnel in effort to take leaked data offline
articles.summary:
The Department of Homeland Security asked an Icelandic hosting company to take down data obtained through hack

The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) asked ⁠an Icelandic hosting…

blocks.text: The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) asked ⁠an Icelandic hosting company on Thursday to take down or limit access to data related to thousands ⁠of agency personnel, saying ⁠the content ​put them at risk, according to the request posted online by hosting company FlokiNET.
The database “places more than ⁠40,000 identifiable individuals at risk of harassment, stalking and physical harm”, the request said.
ZeroFox, a company authorized by the US ⁠Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency to pursue content removal actions, cited the figure in ​an email to FlokiNET.

FlokiNET’s ‌CEO, Kolja Weber, told ‌Reuters that his company would not remove the DHS data because it ‌included government employee work addresses and work phone numbers, not personal phone numbers and addresses.

A DHS spokesperson said the agency “is aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively. We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously ‌and will work to ensure all are properly protected.”

The non-profit data transparency group DDoSecrets released data on more than 40,000 DHS personnel ​on its website on Wednesday, alongside a separate, searchable database developed by hacker and journalist “maia arson crimew”. The database was briefly inaccessible on Thursday but was soon republished at a different domain.

A group calling itself “the Department of Peace” claimed responsibility ⁠for obtaining the data, and said in a statement on Wednesday ​that DHS ​employees “have our information, so it’s only ​fair that we have theirs” and that it hoped ​the data “can be ‌used to limit ​further harm ​by the DHS and supports all efforts in that direction”.
Privacy advocates have criticized the DHS’s use of personal data from other agencies, including Medicaid records and taxpayer data, for immigration enforcement.

articles.title: Iraq: Life sentences for 3 French 'Islamic State' suspects
articles.summary: The three were among 47 French "Islamic State" suspects transferred from Syrian detention. So far, ten French nationals have received prison terms after being convicted of belonging to the group.

image.caption: Many countries are still grappling with how to treat citizens stranded after the so-called Islamic State collapsedImage: Baderkhan Ahmad/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Three French nationals on Thursday received sentences of life imprisonment in Iraq after being convicted of joining the so-called "Islamic State" terror group.
The criminal court in Baghdad sentence Charly S., Kamal M, and Amir A. to life terms in prison which amounts to 20 years of imprisonment in Iraq.
What more do we know?

The trio were found guilty of "the crime of joining the terrorist Islamic State organisation and of having contributed, together with members of the group, to spreading terror," an AFP correspondent said.
Tuesday saw another six French nationals from the same group sentenced to life in prison and a seventh to 15 years for belonging ​to the Islamist militant group.
All of the French nationals sentenced thus far belong to a group of 47 French nationals who were transferred from detention in Syria last year.
The 'Islamic State's' years of terror in Syria and Iraq
The militant group carried out a campaign of terror as it sought to establish a self-proclaimed caliphate in Iraq and Syria from 2014 under its leader, Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi.
Thousands of foreign nationals from across the world joined the group, which carried out mass executions and other atrocities, many of them filmed and shared on social media platforms.

Among its most heinous crimes was the capture and killing of thousands of Yazidis in Iraq’s northern Sinjar region. Many Yazidi women and children were forced into sexual slavery and other forms of enslavement.
In 2014, IS also captured and killed hundreds of Iraqi military cadets at Camp Speicher in Iraq's Tikrit in 2014, much of the massacre filmed and shared on social media.
The terror group also carried out a series of executions of Western journalists and aid workers in highly choreographed videos as part of its media campaign.

Iraq, backed by US-led forces, proclaimed victory over IS in 2017, and along with the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces would go on to ultimately defeat the group territorially in Syria two years later.
The remaining fighters were eventually cornered and defeated in Baghouz in Syria's eastern Deir Ezzor, near the Iraqi border in March, 2019.
UN takes over Syria's Al Hol displacement camp

articles.title: Israeli opposition accuses Netanyahu of trying to 'delegitimise' election
articles.summary: The PM's Likud party has alleged foreign interference and said Arab-led parties "stole" the election after his coalition lost its majority.

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
Activists with a placard saying "Love your neighbour" urge opposition figure Gadi Eisenkot to try to form government that includes Arab-led parties
ByTom Bennett
Reporting fromJerusalem

The main Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot and Arab-led party leaders have denounced Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for alleging foreign interference following the election which saw his coalition lose its majority.
Netanyahu's Likud accused Israel's Arab-led parties of "stealing" the election. Home security agency Shin Bet is investigating whether they received illegal funding from Qatar and Turkey.
Qatar's foreign ministry denied the "ridiculous and dangerous" allegations and accused Israeli politicians of conducting a disinformation campaign against Doha.
Final results confirmed that neither Netanyahu's bloc nor the Jewish opposition had won a majority in parliament.
The two Arab party lists - The Joint List and the Ra'am - defied expectations to win a record 19 seats in the 120-seat Knesset following a surge in turnout among Arab voters.
That positions them as potential kingmakers, with Netanyahu's bloc winning 53 seats and his rival Gadi Eisenkot's bloc securing 48.

On Thursday Likud alleged that voters had been "bribed" to vote for Arab parties, after the head of the Central Elections Committee (CEC) asked the Shin Bet security service to investigate "serious suspicions" of foreign interference.
Both Arab parties strongly rejected the claim, with the Arab-majority Joint List alliance saying it was baseless.

The row is being seen by Netanyahu's critics as an attempt to delegitimise the Arab parties, thereby making it politically impossible for Eisenkot to join forces with them - which is currently his bloc's only route to power.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Arab-led parties including the Joint List headed by Yousef Jabareen (C) won a record 19 seats and could play a kingmaker role

blocks.text: Image source, EPA
Arab-led parties including the Joint List headed by Yousef Jabareen (C) won a record 19 seats and could play a kingmaker role

Israeli media reported that the CEC had been presented with a claim that Qatar had provided funding aimed at increasing voter turnout in Arab communities. Qatar's Foreign Ministry "categorically" denied the claims.
Netanyahu and his Likud Party framed the allegations as a "political earthquake" and an "an attack on democracy", aimed at removing their right-wing government.

But the Shin Bet later clarified that their investigation did not implicate an entire community who had voted legally, while acting CEC Director General Dean Livne said there was "no basis for allegations of systematic violations of election integrity."

Eisenkot, who was briefed on the investigation, said "it is too early to determine what happened, or if anything happened at all," and accused Netanyahu of running "an orchestrated and organized campaign to delegitimize the election results".

Balad chairman Sami Abu Shehadeh, who is part of the Joint List, dismissed the allegation, saying: "The losing side is constructing a racist blood libel and calling on the security agencies to use force in order to overturn the election results."

Netanyahu's attacks on Arab voters and parties have been ongoing for days. He spent much of election day posting on social media that high Arab turnout is an "emergency" and a "matter of life or death" for the Israeli right. He also shared AI-generated images of Arab voters at polling stations, in an attempt to encourage right-wingers to get out and vote.
Netanyahu shares AI image on day of Israeli election
Arab Israelis, many of whom refer to themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel, make up about one fifth of the country.

For years, many boycotted Israeli elections, saying voting would legitimise a system that they say treats them as second-class citizens. But their turnout on Tuesday was inspired by a desire to oust the most right-wing governing coalition in Israel's history, led by Netanyahu.

The final results offer only three plausible options for a government to be formed: a national unity government involving Netanyahu and Eisenkot, a right-wing coalition involving Netanyahu and defectors from Eisenkot's bloc, or an Eisenkot-led government supported by the Arab parties.
Eisenkot and every member of his bloc bar one has previously refused to enter government with Arab parties, but speculation has swirled in recent days that an agreement could yet be reached.

A snap poll conducted by Hebrew University showed that the most popular option for voters from every party in the opposition bloc was for Eisenkot to form a minority government with Ra'am, and supported from outside by the Joint List.

articles.title: Patrick Stewart, Star Trek actor and acclaimed thespian, dies aged 86
articles.summary: Star Trek: the Next Generation and X-Men actor died at his home after ‘a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia’

blocks.text: Patrick Stewart, the acclaimed British stage and screen actor renowned for both Shakespeare and sci-fi, has died. He was 86.

The Star Trek: the Next Generation and X-Men star died on Wednesday at his home in Los Angeles after “a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia”, said Kelly Bush Novak, his longtime spokesperson, to the Hollywood Reporter.

“He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all,” she wrote. “We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace.”

With his authoritative baritone voice and commanding visage, Stewart was already a staple of the British stage by the late 1980s when, at 47, he was cast as a graying Capt Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: the Next Generation, the first live-action spin-off of the groundbreaking 1960s TV series. Over seven seasons aboard the Starship Enterprise, Stewart’s even-keeled performance and steely directives – “engage!” and “make it so” – turned him into a global star.

Stewart reprised his role in four feature film spin-offs – Star Trek Generations (1994), Star Trek: First Contact (1996), Star Trek: Insurrection (1998) and Star Trek: Nemesis (2002) – as well as the TV series Star Trek: Picard, which ran from 2020 until 2023.

His other most well-known role was playing Prof Charles Xavier in the X-Men series. The actor had found work hard to obtain after feeling typecast as a result of his Star Trek role but had been intrigued by working with director Bryan Singer for 2000’s X-Men.

blocks.caption: Patrick Stewart in X-Men 2. Photograph: MARVEL/Allstar

blocks.text: He went on to play the role in seven films and will be seen reprising the role in this December’s Avengers: Doomsday.

Marvel chief Kevin Feige has paid tribute in a statement calling him “brilliant, charming, warm, generous, with a quiet strength and gravitas”. He added: “Away from the cameras, he was even more remarkable, with a wonderfully sharp sense of humor. It was a true privilege to know him and to work with him. His legacy lives on not only in decades of extraordinary work, but in the many, many people he mentored. He will be deeply missed.”
His other film roles included gay comedy Jeffrey, romantic thriller Conspiracy Theory, violent horror Green Room and voice roles in Ted, Gnomeo & Juliet and, most recently, The Sheep Detectives.

Born on 13 July 1940 in the small industrial village of Mirfield, England, Stewart was the youngest of three sons born to Alfred Stewart, a British military veteran turned semiskilled laborer, and Gladys Stewart, a weaver at a textile factory. His childhood, in a small house with no running hot water, was marred by alcoholism and domestic violence, a situation he later described, in an article for the Guardian from 2009, as “barely tolerable”.

He found respite in acting, first in school – he was 12 when an English teacher assigned him the part of Shylock in Shakespeare’s the Merchant of Venice – and then local drama groups. “I managed to find my own refuge in acting,” he wrote. “The stage was a far safer place for me than anything I had to live through at home – it offered escape. I could be someone else, in another place, in another time.”

After graduating from secondary school at 15, he worked as a local reporter and furniture salesman before a local arts council provided the funding to attend the prestigious Bristol Old Vic Theater School, where he enrolled in 1957, at 17. Having shed his Yorkshire accent, he took his first professional theater role two years later, and in 1966 joined the Royal Shakespeare Company.
Throughout his career, he won a Grammy award and two Laurence Olivier awards for his stage work. He was also nominated for a Tony and four Emmys.
In 2023, he also released his memoir called Making It So.

“I think I’ve been in denial about my life for a very long time,” he said to the Guardian in a 2023 interview. “I never really took on board how successful I had become. Even today I sometimes think, ‘You’re a lucky son of a bitch, Patrick,’ when something unexpected or good happens to me.”

articles.title: 'The city is alive': A brief peace in Kherson, but residents fear what comes next
articles.summary: A temporary ceasefire has brought rare quiet to Kherson, offering its residents a glimpse of normal life before fighting resumes.

blocks.text: The Ukrainian city of Kherson has known its first two days of quiet after many years, as a US-brokered temporary ceasefire has allowed residents rare moments of respite from the constant Russian aerial attacks that plague the front line region.

Videos posted on social media showed people strolling down streets covered in anti-drone nets and gathering in the city's squares - ordinary activities that usually mean keeping one eye on the sky and one ear out for incoming drones.
"Ever since the ceasefire was announced, there's been total silence," said Olga, 42, speaking by phone from Kherson. "We are all, of course, overjoyed."
"I don't even know what to call it," she added, her smile coming through in her voice. "It's as if everything has finally come to an end."
Since Tuesday, Kherson has "literally come back to life," Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said.
"People are calmly going out, walking, enjoying the autumn sun. What for some is ordinary everyday life, for residents of the Kherson region today is the greatest desire."

The temporary pause in hostilities - due to end on Sunday - is the result of efforts by US First Lady Melania Trump to broker a safe passage out of the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky, which lies on the other side of the Dnipro river from Kherson.
For several days, Russian forces have been working to clear the road of mines, ahead of a planned evacuation of Oleshky's civilians on Friday.

But there are fears that, alongside carrying out the well-publicised "humanitarian operation" – which some American journalists will be invited to witness – the Russians are using the truce to bolster their forces in the area ahead of a renewed onslaught of Kherson from next week.

"They are... using this lull to strengthen their positions, bring in more military supplies, weapons, ammunition, and drones, and carry out some redeployment of their forces," an anonymous source working in local government told the BBC.

Petro Andriushchenko, Director of Ukraine's Center for Studying the Occupation, says Kherson locals have told him that they witnessed a military build-up around Radensk, some 20km (12 miles) from Oleshky.

Its residents will be saved but "we are simultaneously giving the enemy an opportunity to exploit the ceasefire for its own military purposes," he said. Once the ceasefire ends, the situation may be "worse than we saw before, because Russia's units will be stronger. They have enough time to prepare to prolong this action."
Though Kherson residents are clear-eyed about what lies ahead, for a brief period this week the city caught its breath.
No violations have been reported on either side since Tuesday. There have been other ceasefires in the past, but these were generally not respected, Kherson resident Dima said.
"This is the first time the shelling has stopped, people don't quite believe it," he told the BBC. "They are going to the shops, drinking coffee, walking around... The city is alive."

On social media, a woman named Yulia wrote about her unusually uneventful trip to the supermarket with an edge of disbelief. For once, she said, she returned home from the shops "whole and calm, not as usual - scared, sweating from the horror and with a lump in my throat."

This week, dozens of people were also able to access their belongings and homes in the so-called "red zone" of Kherson – an area so exposed to drones and artillery attacks that it has become unlivable.

"Some are venturing into places where nobody has dared to go for years, filming areas where simply being present has meant - and will once again mean - almost certain death," said Denisa Bohackova, a Czech volunteer who lives in Kherson.
Dima described scenes of "girls, boys, parents, grandmothers" walking down the streets of the red zone carrying suitcases and bags, returning to their flats to see what they could retrieve.

Some of those who returned to the red zone found buildings reduced to charred, empty shells; in other cases, homes had been looted. The scale of destruction in some of these places, Bohackova said, is "breathtaking".

Others were rushing back for reasons beyond material concerns. Angela Dobrovolska's husband Serhiy was killed two years ago by a grenade dropped by a piloted Russian drone - an instance of a "human safari" attack of the kind that Kherson has become sadly infamous for.

On Thursday, Angela headed back from Kyiv to Kherson to visit his grave for the first time in months. "They say that all the people have rushed to Kherson," she said. "And I'll be going to the cemetery to my husband."
The population of Kherson has dwindled from over 250,000 to about 65,000 since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, which will enter its sixth year in February.

Though civilian life in the city never stopped, Bohackova said, it also carried on under the conditions of an active battlefield, with schools, theatres, kindergartens and hospitals moved underground.
"An ordinary civilian from Kherson has experienced more of this war than many soldiers," Bohackova said.
Olga, who is raising two children, described regular blackouts, mines dropped by drones and concealed by fallen leaves, drone fragments ricocheting, and a city that typically shuts by the afternoon.

But since silence fell on the city, Olga has been able to live a normal life. She drove to a different town and took the bus to another district to visit her grandmother with her son. Around her, the shops were full, as were the cafes. After years of quiet streets, "there was even a small traffic jam," she smiled.
But the clock is ticking.
The evacuation of nearby Oleshky is due to be completed by Sunday, after which the ceasefire will be over. "The concern is that, starting Monday, things could turn truly chaotic," Olga said.
"We know the strikes will resume, and that they will increase," said Dima, as he and his wife prepared to visit their flat in the red zone for the first time in several months.
"These few days showed us how it could be if it all finally ended."

articles.title: Healey backs away from cutting welfare cost despite warnings of public finance shortfall
articles.summary:
Experts round on chancellor over ‘scattergun’ budget, saying he ducked big tax and spending decisions

John Healey has backed away from cutting the cost of welfare this parliament, amid dire…

blocks.text: John Healey has backed away from cutting the cost of welfare this parliament, amid dire warnings his first budget could lead to brutal spending cuts because of a £28bn shortfall in public finances.
Experts rounded on Healey’s steady-as-she-goes budget on Thursday, with the Institute for Fiscal Studies saying he had left himself a mountain to climb by ducking big tax and spending decisions.

In a damning analysis, the IFS said Healey would need to have set aside an additional £28bn a year, to offset the impact of inflation on future spending plans and hit the target of spending 3% of GDP in defence by 2030.
Instead Helen Miller, the IFS director, said Healey had opened the way to “a spending review that looks pretty brutal for some departments” – including real-term budget cuts.

“Public service spending plans look extremely tight. They don’t look to me like plans that this government would want to deliver,” she said, adding that meant Healey could face, “another season of damaging speculation about tax rises”.

The welfare bill will not be part of the spending review, which focuses on departmental budgets. But in a bid to underline his determination to balance the books, the chancellor pointed to plans for reform, telling BBC Radio 4’s Today: “We have to bring the benefits bill down.”

He had earlier appeared to say cuts would be made in this parliament, when asked if there would be a reduction in the bill before the next election. “There will be. There will be a reduction in the benefits bill,” said Healey. “We’ll do that in a Labour way and we will do that because it is simply not good for Britain or progress to have a bigger and bigger benefits bill.”

However, Treasury officials clarified that he had not meant to give a timeline and Healey later told Channel 4: “It’s not correct to say that we are going to bring this welfare bill down in this parliament because we’ve not set a timetable for that.”
Instead, he pointed to forthcoming reviews from Alan Milburn on employment support for young people, and from Stephen Timms, on disability benefits.
Milburn is expected to recommend additional spending upfront, aimed at bringing down costs over the longer term by helping more young people into employment.

The Office for Budget Responsibility has said total welfare spending will grow from £334bn last year to £431bn by 2030 – with about half of that being spent on pensioners and a quarter on sickness and disability benefits. The overall forecast spending has risen by £8bn since March.
With a tough global economic backdrop, Healey has said the single biggest driver of better prospects for the UK would be for an end to the Iran and Ukraine wars.

But in his interviews, Healey appeared to take a more cautious view on the potential for growth from rejoining Europe or the single market than the prime minister. Asked by LBC if growth would be stronger if the UK were in the EU or the single market, Healey replied: “Well, I don’t actually accept that. Brexit has certainly hit our level of growth. It’s certainly hit our level of trade. But we had a referendum. We’re out of the European Union. The challenge for me now is how do we make the best of an economy which this year has proved remarkably resilient.”
Asked later by Channel 4 if he, like Andy Burnham, hoped for the UK to reenter the bloc in his lifetime, Healey said: “I’m older than Andy Burnham. I don’t expect to see that.”

The chancellor put measures to ease the cost of living at the heart of his first budget, including a £100 winter cost of living payment for most households. However, critics lined up on Thursday to accuse him of taking a “scattergun” approach – and of not hitting Britain’s banks hard enough to fund the package.

The Resolution Foundation thinktank said Healey had failed to target energy support to the households that need it most ahead of a difficult winter, with bills expected to rise sharply in January and the Bank of England to raise interest rates next week.

Ruth Curtice, Resolution’s chief executive, said: “Faced with a tough backdrop amid global economic turmoil, the chancellor delivered a scattergun budget that did little to address the sharp challenges facing Britain.
“Cost of living support is being spread far too thinly and will leave even those families receiving help facing higher energy bills than they did during the last energy price shock.”
Paul Nowak, the TUC’s general secretary, has strongly advocated for a bank windfall tax to fund energy support. He said he welcomed Healey’s approach, but would be pushing for him to go further.

The chancellor has doubled the surcharge banks pay on their profits from 3% to 6% for 15 months. Novak said: “It was right to tax banks to help people with their energy bills, but I think banks could have been asked to pay a fairer share. He’s going to review it in 15 months. We’re going to be looking as part of that review – if banks are still making windfall profits – for him to extend and increase the bank tax.”

As well as casting doubt on whether Healey’s future spending plans are realistic, the IFS said the £15bn headroom, or buffer, he has left himself against Labour’s fiscal rules could easily be eroded by higher than expected energy costs.

The chancellor allowed the buffer to absorb some of the impact of the Iran war, which has driven up the government’s cost of borrowing. At the time of the spring statement, Rachel Reeves had built up headroom of £24bn.
Miller said that was a “reasonable” decision to make, but “a lower buffer leaves the chancellor more exposed to future bad news”.

articles.title: What's the deal with question period? Poilievre, MacKinnon trade Seinfeld-related barbs
articles.summary: Regular question period viewers got a little more than the usual "yada, yada, yada" on Thursday as Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre and Government House leader Steven MacKinnon traded…

blocks.text: Politics·New

Regular question period viewers got a little more than the usual "yada, yada, yada" on Thursday as Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre and Government House leader Steven MacKinnon traded Seinfeld-related jabs.
Seinfeld references dominated opening round of Thursday's session
Poilievre, MacKinnon trade Seinfeld-themed blows in question period
Poilievre kicked off the reference contest with a question about the Canada-EU summit taking place in Montreal this week.
"Is this just another Seinfeld summit? A meeting about nothing?" Poilievre asked, referencing the '90s sitcom that was billed as a show "about nothing."
MacKinnon shot back at Poilievre by riffing on a line from the hit show, saying that the opposition leader "lives the same recurring nightmare every single day."
The cast of Seinfeld poses at the Screen Actors Guild Awards in 1995. (Reuters)

The Conservative leader kept the references going by arguing that Prime Minister Mark Carney acts like Jason Alexander's character George Costanza, "running around the office trying to look busy while achieving nothing at all in the real world."
MacKinnon then tried to cast Poilievre as another character, Cosmo Kramer, suggesting that the Conservative leader "just walks into the room every time and says something weird."
The sitcom went off the air in 1998 after nine seasons.
The back-and-forth comes as Carney is meeting with representatives of the European Union in an effort to strengthen ties with the 27-member bloc.
EU agreement 'names or nomenclature' don't matter, says Carney
While the prime minister has insisted that the substance of a new agreement with the EU is what matters, questions have swirled around what the label of the new alliance will be.

CBC News reported on Wednesday that words "associate membership" were removed from a joint statement expected to be released at the summit, but that hasn't stopped European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen from using that branding.

Conservatives have continuously raised questions about what a closer relationship with the EU would mean. Poilievre says Carney should focus on getting nine laggard countries to ratify the Canada-European Union Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Darren Major is a senior writer for CBC's parliamentary bureau in Ottawa. He previously worked as a digital reporter for CBC Ottawa and a producer for CBC's Power & Politics. He holds a master's degree in journalism and a bachelor's degree in public affairs and policy management, both from Carleton University. He also holds a master's degree in arts from Queen's University. He can be reached at darren.major@cbc.ca.

articles.title: JD Vance letter may offer last chance to avert fresh conflict between US and Iran
articles.summary:
US vice-president writes to top Iranian security official in sign Washington has not abandoned diplomacy

Lingering hopes of averting a major new conflagration between Iran and the US soon…

blocks.text: Lingering hopes of averting a major new conflagration between Iran and the US soon after Tuesday’s midterm elections could rest on Iran’s response to a personal letter from the US vice-president, JD Vance, offering to restart diplomacy.

The letter, written after predominantly Qatari mediation, was sent to the secretary of Iran’s supreme national security council, Mohsen Rezaei on Sunday and requires Tehran to agree to make commitments on its nuclear programme at the start of a process that would lead to the opening of the strait of Hormuz within seven days in return for US sanctions relief.

A reply is imminent, but Iran is reluctant to give upfront and irreversible commitments on its nuclear programme, such as exporting its stockpile of highly enriched uranium to a third country, if the compensatory US steps, such as lifting sanctions on Iranian oil exports, are reversible.
Some form of third-party guarantee that both sides will adhere to their commitments has been discussed, with China often mentioned as the only country of sufficient status to underwrite it.
The return of Vance, a sceptic about the war, to the negotiations is significant and a sign that the US has not abandoned diplomacy.

blocks.caption: An anti-US mural in Tehran. Photograph: Abedin Taherkenareh/EPA

blocks.text: One Democrat senator briefed on the targets the US military had identified in Iran said described the plan for a renewed attack as “insane and likely lead to the destruction of our commitment to the rule of law”.

In a sign of Iran’s reluctance to meet US demands about sequencing, its chief negotiator, Mohammad Ghalibaf, wrote on X: “Iran’s conditions have been repeatedly and clearly stated to the mediators. The carrot-and-stick approach has no effect on Iran. Progress can only be achieved once Iran’s seven conditions have been agreed upon.”
Those conditions include the lifting of sanctions, ending asset freezes and the end to the war on all fronts, a phrase that requires an Israeli ceasefire in Lebanon.

The US wants front-loaded, specific commitments about the removal of Iran’s stockpile of highly-enriched uranium. Tehran is reluctant to give up its bargaining leverage, and also resists the return of UN nuclear inspectors for fear they might provide the US with intelligence on the whereabouts and state of the stockpile.
It has proposed blending the stockpile down inside Iran so it is no longer useable to make a nuclear weapon.

The Vance letter was sent to Rezaei rather than Ghalibaf or the foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, because Washington judged that decision-making power rests with those closest to the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps. In practice, Iran tries to reach decisions through consensus at the highest level of government in a six strong committee.

blocks.caption: The secretary of Iran’s supreme national security council, Mohsen Rezaei.  Photograph: Mohammed Salem/Reuters

blocks.text: Ghalibaf and Rezaei met the supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, last week to discuss the risk of a new war. Khamenei has said he would like an end to the current state of no war, no peace. Iran has well laid plans ready to strike back against US interests in the region by hitting desalination plants, internet cables and electricity grids across the Gulf.

For a third US attack in two years to have any rationale or prospect of inducing Iran’s capitulation, the plan would require the US, probably in conjunction with a caretaker government in Israel, to mount attacks on previously off-limits targets. Europe would not join the attacks, but the views of the Gulf states, the chief targets of Iran reprisals, would be key.

The Connecticut senator Chris Murphy told a briefing at the Middle East Institute: “I did get a fairly detailed conversation about what the war plan would be … I will just say this their plan is insane. It will lead to devastating escalation and the likely destruction of our commitment to the rule of law.

“There has been open reporting as to the civilian infrastructure we may be targeting … I think the plan they have developed will lead in my judgement to a prolongment [sic] and escalation of this war that will be devastating to our security interest”.

Although Tehran trusts Vance marginally more than most White House politicians and envoys, the Iranian high command is still suspicious about his status after he negotiated a 14-point memorandum of understanding which then fell apart when other members of the US administration took charge of its implementation.

That led to unilateral US steps to reopen the strait of Hormuz that Iran said contravened the terms of the agreement. Trump also came to detest it because it delayed the start of nuclear talks for as long as 60 days.

In an offer made by Tehran on the margins of the UN general assembly, it proposed foreshortening the timeframe before nuclear talks started, saying they could start withinsix or seven days of the US restoring the sanctions waiver on its oil exports and the reopening of the strait of Hormuz.

articles.title: 'No sugar-coating it': NDP ex-ministers admit frustration at snap election blunder
articles.summary: Two prominent figures in British Columbia's outgoing NDP government have spoken out about the scale of the mistake made in calling last weekend's election that resulted in the party's crushing defeat.

image.caption: Niki Sharma, who was previously attorney general, speaks with reporters at the B.C. Legislature on Thursday, Oct. 29, 2026. (CBC News)

blocks.text: British Columbia

Two prominent figures in British Columbia's outgoing NDP government have spoken out about the scale of the mistake made in calling last weekend's election that resulted in the party's crushing defeat.
Both Ravi Parmar and Niki Sharma leave door open to NDP leadership run

Niki Sharma and Ravi Parmar are both leaving open the possibility they may seek party leadership in the wake of the resignation of outgoing Premier David Eby, as the decimated NDP caucus meets at the legislature.
Sharma, who was previously attorney general, says Eby apologized for calling the snap election at a meeting of the outgoing caucus on Wednesday, and he "took full responsibility."

items: Wounded B.C. NDP caucus meets after humbling election defeat

blocks.text: She says she's not seeking the interim leadership of the party, a position that is being discussed at today's meeting of the incoming caucus, but was non-committal on the permanent leadership.

Parmar, the outgoing forests minister, says the party and Eby clearly made the wrong decision to call the election that resulted in a two-thirds majority of 63 seats for the B.C. Conservatives, while the NDP ranks have been reduced from 47 to 28, according to the preliminary count.
Parmar says the party "got it wrong" and owes British Columbians an apology for calling the election, while adding that it's too early to say if he'll seek leadership.

"The premier made a decision, we all stood by him … clearly we made the wrong decision calling the election, and that's something that we're all going to live by," he said before the start of the caucus meeting.
Outgoing B.C. NDP MLA says party has ‘lost their way’ after massive election loss
Asked to rate the level of frustration at the election call, Parmar said it was "about 10, absolutely."
"I'm disappointed, I'm frustrated, but that disappointment and frustration can't last four years, it can only last a few days," he said.
Sharma said that Wednesday's outgoing caucus meeting was an emotional affair, as colleagues bid farewell to each other.
"There's no sugar-coating it. It was a tough day. We had to say goodbye to MLAs that were excellent, that really served their community well," she said.
"So we were reflective, and I think there's a resolve within that reflectiveness to figure out how we do the job that British Columbia has elected us to do now, which is as official Opposition."

articles.title: You can see You Can See Everything everywhere
articles.summary: The documentary You Can See Everything about Elizabeth Holmes is a box-office hit, an awards season contender and a social media obsession.

image.caption: This composite shows Jimmy Fallon, from left, and Jamie Lee Curtis on The Tonight Show parodying Nathan Fielder and Elizbeth Holmes from the film, You Can See Everything. (NBC/A24)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New
The documentary You Can See Everything about Elizabeth Holmes is a box-office hit, an awards season contender and a social media obsession.
Elizabeth Holmes, Theranos founder and convicted fraudster, has become a meme machine
Some movies leave you with a memorable line. You Can See Everything leaves you with a face inches from yours and plenty of parodies.

Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim's movie about Elizabeth Holmes, Theranos founder and convicted fraudster, has become a meme machine, powered by the film's most unnerving visual signature: close talking. Online, the answer has been to turn the pauses, the proximity, the dead-serious eye contact and that discomfort into a format.

items: You Can See Everything sells out theatres, and people can't stop talking about it
Loved You Can See Everything? Thank Canada

blocks.text: The latest take came on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon, where Jamie Lee Curtis played Holmes and Fallon took on Fielder. They delivered a shot-for-shot remake of of one of the film's most intense exchanges.

With tense music underneath, Fallon mirrored Fielder's measured questions and subtle expressions while Curtis held Holmes's wide-eyed stare and repeated her lines, including, "I'm engaging with you as a human being." The pair stayed in character until Fallon walked away and Curtis broke the tension.
The spoof quickly won over viewers online, with fans calling it Emmy-worthy and some saying Fallon looked so much like Fielder they briefly thought it was him.
This Hour Has 22 Minutes borrows the film's close-talking tension for a parody negotiation between U.S. President Donald Trump and Prime Minister Mark Carney.
As Trump insists he isn't lying, Carney asks, "So you won't try to make Canada the 51st state?"
Trump promises he won't, then admits, "I lied."
Their face-to-face exchange spirals into an absurd argument about truth and trust, with Carney struggling to follow Trump's shifting story.

The joke made its way to Washington Square Park in New York City, where dozens gathered for a Holmes and Fielder lookalike contest. Organized by comedian Maddy West and a friend, the event drew more than 200 registration responses.

The winners were Nicole Travolta, an actor and comedian who has been impersonating Holmes since 2022, and Joe Sivick, whose resemblance to Fielder was convincing enough to briefly fool one of the organizers.
Fans react online

On platforms including X, Instagram, TikTok and Reddit, users have also been reacting to Holmes and Fielder's real-life exchanges, even making parodies of their own. One Reddit user reimagined the film as You Can Eat Anything.
Other memes transplant the film's dead-serious dialogue into everyday situations. One X user posted, "It's finally fall, we're going apple picking with my college friends next Sunday at 1 pm."
A user on Reddit re-shared this one, which said, "My cat telling me she hasn't been fed yet. Why would I deceive you? There's no reason for me to do that."
A reddit user re-shared this meme that says, 'My cat telling me she hasn't been fed yet. Why would I deceive you? There's no reason for me to do that.' (jhovudi1/Reddit)
Box office success

The film's reach extends beyond social media. It took in more than $15 million US during its opening weekend, the second-largest opening weekend for a non-musical documentary in domestic box office history, behind only 2004's Fahrenheit 9/11.

It's also currently the highest-rated movie in Rotten Tomatoes history, currently sitting at 97 per cent fresh. The audience response has also prompted A24 to mount an ambitious Oscars campaign, seeking consideration for You Can See Everything in categories including best picture and best director — an unprecedented push for a feature documentary.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Christine Pagulayan is a Toronto-based producer and writer with CBC News, currently with the Entertainment unit. She has worked in various roles at CBC News Network and The National. She has also worked as a multiplatform reporter in Toronto, Winnipeg, Halifax and Moncton. You can reach her at christine.pagulayan@cbc.ca.
With files from Helen Surgenor

articles.title: Seven oil tankers carrying 288,000 tonnes of Russian diesel sail towards US
articles.summary:
Tankers, tracked by Greenpeace, are first phase of Trump-Putin deal – but there is uncertainty over whether they will unload

Seven oil tankers carrying an estimated 288,000 tonnes of Russian…
articles.byline: Dan Sabbagh Defence and security editor

blocks.text: Seven oil tankers carrying an estimated 288,000 tonnes of Russian diesel are now sailing towards the US, though it is uncertain if the vessels will be able to unload amid a political row about the legality of the shipments.

The transport, tracked by the pressure group Greenpeace, is the first phase of a contentious supply deal negotiated between presidents Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin earlier this month, reversing years of sanctions on Russia oil.

Previous reports had counted three tankers that had departed Russian oil terminals in the Baltic Sea, but using a range of sources, including shipping tracking websites, Greenpeace believes its monitoring exercise is the most complete yet.

Shaun Burnie, an energy specialist with Greenpeace Ukraine, argued that now the location of the tankers could be plotted on a map, the shipments should be halted by Congress or local authorities in the US.
“Instead of rewarding Russia for its vile war against Ukraine, there needs to be more punitive sanctions against Russia,” he said. “These shipments can be stopped”.

One of the seven tankers, Taurus, is relatively close to the US, but at the time the map was first published, five of the others were close to the UK, and three were sailing through or into the English Channel.

In Ukraine, 14 people were reported killed on Thursday morning when a Russian drone struck a crowded train platform in the central city of Dnipro. Five others were reported killed in daytime strikes in two other cities, Chernihiv and Kremenchuk.

Ukrzaliznytsia, Ukraine’s state railway company, said a high speed jet-powered drone had struck as a commuter train was preparing to depart Dnipro’s main station. Bodies lay scattered after the relatively unusual daytime attack, which took place at around 11am.

Putin agreed to supply the US with 1.8m tonnes of diesel in a surprise deal announced on 9 October, starting with 300,000 tonnes immediately. Trump announced a six-month waiver on existing sanctions to allow the shipments to proceed.

Russia had been hit by waves of economic sanctions from the US, EU, UK and other leading western economies since Putin launched the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. But this autumn, Trump has altered course and tried to work more closely with Putin, even though Russia has not stopped attacking its neighbour.

blocks.caption: Emergency workers at the scene of a purported Russian drone attack on Dnipro’s main station on Thursday. Photograph: Reuters

blocks.text: Earlier this week, a group of US lawmakers, led by a handful of Democratic senators, warned banks and port authorities that they could face congressional investigations and other legal action if they handled the Russian diesel.

Mikie Sherrill, the Democratic governor of New Jersey, said she was looking at how to prevent the diesel from being unloaded, if an attempt was made to do so in her state. She described the deal as “corrupt and illegal”.

There have been reports that the White House has been trying to encourage US firms to take the oil, though it is not clear buyers are forthcoming, given the legal risks so close to next Tuesday’s midterm elections.

Trump’s popularity has waned as fuel prices in the US have soared since he attacked Iran in the spring. Polling suggests a high likelihood that control of the House of Representatives could pass to the Democrats in the elections, while the battle over the Senate is considered too close to call.

The US president had argued that the Russia deal would help lower diesel prices, though the price per gallon has risen from $6.28 at the time the agreement was announced to $6.33, according to the American Automobile Association.

Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, denounced the agreement because the money raised would help the Kremlin fund the ongoing war. “Backroom deals” gave Putin more chances on the battlefield, he said.

The Kremlin has been trying to keep information about the latest oil exports secret. A presidential decree from the end of September restricted the publication of information about oil exports in an effort to evade international sanctions.

articles.title: EU seeks 'highest level' ties with Canada in Montreal summit
articles.summary: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said EU seeks "association without accession" for Canada, after EU members snub "associate member" designation.

image.caption: The EU is seeking to build a partnership "closer to membership than anything we have done before," Ursula von der Leyen said.Image: Anne Pollmann/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: European Union and Canadian leaders met on Thursday during a summit in Montreal, at a special Canada-EU summit to discuss critical policies like artificial inteligence (AI), climate, energy and ⁠security.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the EU will continue to explore Canada's prospects for becoming the bloc's first "associate member."
But despite her comments, the summit's declaration is expected to exclude the term "associate member," a move pushed by Germany and other members.
"Our idea is simple: it is an association without accession," Von der Leyen clarified. "We can build a partnership that comes closer to membership than anything we have done before."
"We both want to bring our relationship to the highest level possible," von der Leyen added.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney had said this week he wasn't concerned about the "associate member" status, or "specific names" to be given to the new alliance with the EU.
"What matters is the difference that it will make to the lives of Canadians," Carney added.
Canada's EU ties are part of a broader strategy, expert tells DW
Ottawa's quest for deeper ties to Europe is seen as a move to reduce its reliance on the US since President Donald Trump imposed tariffs on a range of Canadian goods.

Frederic Merand, political expert on EU-Canada relations at the University of Montreal, spoke to DW about how the summit serves as "political impetus" to improve the bilateral trade relationship and to free Canada of its reliance on the US.

"It's not going to happen, over time, overnight. And every time we move closer to the Europeans, we realize how dependent we are on the US and how also vulnerable we are to, for example, us retaliation," Merand said.

But he added that courting the EU is also part of a broader strategy "to reinvent the Canadian economy, to create a single market, to attract more investment," as well as to diversify our partnerships with China, India and also other parts of the world.
The EU is "a natural partner" to work with, Merand said, given its existing free trade agreement with Canada, in addition to the close historical and cultural ties between the two partners.
Are the EU and Canada moving closer?
What's on the agenda for the summit?

An EU official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told AFP that Canada and the EU sought to align policies in areas such as climate, energy and artificial intelligence, allowing Ottawa to participate in some EU programs.
Canada has critical minerals needed for green technologies such as batteries and wind turbines, something for which Europe normally relies on China.
But Canada is in need of major infrastructure investment to develop its mining industry.
There are hopes that the summit can result in a plan for the European Investment Bank to back Canadian critical mineral projects.
EU and Canadian leaders are also looking into a digital trade deal that can allow for faster and cheaper online transactions.
Additionally, Canada could be allowed to participate in the EU's Erasmus youth program, which allows university students to spend a semester abroad.

articles.title: Dirty tricks or much ado about nothing? Why Alaska, for once, is front and centre in midterms
articles.summary: Could a manoeuvre reportedly plotted by officials connected to Democratic candidate Mary Peltola backfire and cost the party in its attempt to regain control of the Senate in next week's midterms?…

image.caption: This combination photo shows Sen. Dan Sullivan, left, and Dan J. Sullivan, right. Both will appear on the ballot for a Senate seat in Alaska on Tuesday, despite Washington's objections and Republican accusations of political chicanery by the Democrats. (Mark Thiessen, Becky Bohrer/The Associated Pre

blocks.text: The presence of two candidates named Dan Sullivan on the Alaska ballot for a Senate election has attracted attention for about six months now in U.S. political news coverage.

Right-wing media outlets have suspected it was not a mere coincidence, but an example of chicanery, and an investigation by the New York Times resulted in an article Wednesday that suggests a co-ordinated effort by individuals associated with Democrat Mary Peltola's campaign to recruit anyone with the same name as Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan.
A spokesperson for the Peltola campaign had previously said it had "no involvement with either Sullivan campaign."

While political action committees and campaigns for both parties have occasionally engaged in similar "ballot-stacking" tactics that appeared to have the express purpose of siphoning votes from well-established politicians, the Alaska scenario is perhaps the most high-profile example yet seen.

Attorney General Todd Blanche said Wednesday it "should be" illegal, and U.S. President Donald Trump has suggested that criminal prosecutions should result, without specifying on what grounds, or for which particular individuals.
Here's a look at how we got here and the questions that have emerged ahead of Tuesday's midterms.
The facts

Several candidates appeared on the Senate ballot in the spring, including incumbent Dan Sullivan, whose middle name is Scott. But also on the ballot was Republican Dan J. Sullivan. A retired schoolteacher, he is a neophyte in terms of political office and has registered as a Democrat in the past.

In June, the state's Republican lieutenant-governor disqualified Dan J. Sullivan under a state regulation that forbids ballot names that are "confusing or misleading to voters or compromises the fairness or neutrality of the ballot."

A campaign spokesperson for Democratic Senate hopeful Mary Peltola, seen in Anchorage, Alaska, on Oct. 14, has previously said it had 'no involvement with either Sullivan campaign.' (Becky Bohrer/The Associated Press)

But a state judge's reversal of that decision was upheld by the Alaska Supreme Court. The gist of their ruling was that there is no statutory or constitutional mechanism to remove a person from the ballot if they had met the qualifications to register as a candidate, no matter the origin story of the candidacy.

"There's a lot of different ways you can distinguish these two candidates on the ballot, short of precluding access to the ballot to begin with," Aimee Oravec, an Alaska justice, said during oral arguments in the case.
Why it matters

What the composition of the Senate will look like after its three-dozen races are called is seen as an unpredictable puzzle by pollsters. Republicans hold a 53-47 majority ⁠and Democrats need four pickups to regain control of the chamber, so the race between Peltola and the incumbent Sullivan could be pivotal.
Alaska is one of the smallest electorates. Sullivan was elected to office in 2014 by two percentage points, which translated to just over 6,000 more votes than his opponent.

In the all-party primary in August to determine the top four candidates, the candidate derisively nicknamed "Decoy Dan" by some garnered 4,107 votes, about 2 per cent of the total vote. This despite the fact he's reportedly spent no money on campaign staff or media.

Democrats have defended the manoeuvre as an example of political hardball. They have pointed to examples nationally of Republican-led efforts to place candidates on ballots as a diversionary tactic, and Alaska Democrats alleged in 2024 that Republicans were behind a scheme to get an incarcerated candidate — who's running again this year — on the ballot to siphon votes from their preferred U.S. House candidate.

Peltola and her campaign haven't fully addressed the Times allegations, merely calling it a "diversion." The revelation could backfire for Peltola, a Yup'ik who became the first Indigenous person from Alaska to ever serve in Congress when she won a House seat in 2022.
In addition to Sullivan, Republican Lisa Murkowski, the other U.S. senator from Alaska, is calling for her to come clean about her knowledge of the scheme.

items: U.S. midterms could be the country's most expensive elections yet. To what end?
Why the Hispanic vote could sway the outcome of the U.S. midterm elections

blocks.text: The gambit could also just breed more general cynicism in a country where unfounded allegations of vote fraud in the 2020 election led to a riot at the U.S. Capitol.
"How does this increase voter confidence in our election process?" the Juneau Empire, the newspaper out of the state capital, asked in a recent editorial.
Legal fallout
After the Times article landed, Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy said he was directing the state's Department of Public Safety to investigate the scheme to see if criminal or civil offences occurred.
"Deliberately tricking voters into casting their ballots for someone else strikes at the integrity of our elections," said Dunleavy.
Trump accused of mounting fear-based intimidation campaign ahead of U.S. midterms
Several days before the Times exposé landed, the Justice Department filed a lawsuit to demand that Alaska be blocked from certifying a Peltola win if Dan J. Sullivan remains on the ballot.

Trump said he had ordered the department to do that and no criticism emerged in Congress from Republicans who regularly lobbed accusations about a politicized Justice Department under Democratic predecessor Joe Biden.
Legal questions
It is hard to predict if any criminality occurred, given what is known so far. But vote-siphoning schemes have led to charges for individuals before.

As for the Justice Department suit, the U.S. Constitution grants states the power to run their own elections. Election experts are pessimistic about its chances for success, and even the Trump-friendly Wall Street Journal editorial page called it a "legal Hail Mary."

"The statute simply doesn't let the Department of Justice enjoin certification," Derek Muller, University of Notre Dame law professor, told the Associated Press last week. "The lawsuit could well be mooted by a wide Democratic victory or a narrow Republican one, and if not, the court will likely dismiss it next month."

The lawsuit asks the court to block certification until an investigation determines whether enough voters were fooled in a way that swings the election. It doesn't explain how that would happen, and the right to privacy provides another complication, as votes are supposed to be confidential.

Election expert Rick Hasen called the Times report a "bombshell" and said perjury prosecutions were possible if it could be established someone lied about involvement in the scheme. But Hasen, UCLA law professor and director of the Safeguarding Democracy Project, wrote Wednesday on his blog that he didn't think the new reporting changed the equation on the Justice Department suit.
Hasen also said he didn't see any mechanism for the government to criminalize Dan J. Sullivan's campaign.

"And if it could do so, then it could be a crime every time that the Republican Party backs a Green Party candidate, or Democrats support a MAGA candidate in a primary in the hopes that the candidate would be weaker against a Democrat in the general election," he said.
The ballot wrinkle
A sample election ballot for Alaska shows how the two Sullivan's running for a Senate seat are being distinguished. (Haven Daley/The Associated Press)
Alaska employs a ranked-choice ballot. Some local editorials, as well as the Wall Street Journal, have argued that such a system encourages the possibility of voter confusion and sham candidates.

Democrats counter that the local electorate has likely been inundated for months with stories and video differentiating the two men. In addition, they say, a voter could just simply choose not to rank Peltola at all on their ballot, with the likelihood that the less seasoned Sullivan comes out on top over the man who's represented Alaska for over a decade considered remote.

items: US Politics! Will Texas flip, who's bailing on Trump?
Democrats promise Epstein probes will be a priority if they win midterms, but to what end?

blocks.text: It's not the citizenry's first go-round with the system, which has been in place since 2022. Even Republican Murkowski, criticizing the Justice Department suit last week, has said that "Alaskans don't need any help voting for their preferred candidates."
It is too late to change ballots. Dan J. Sullivan is listed as "Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.," without a party label, and Dan S. Sullivan is listed as "Dan S. Sullivan (Registered Republican) Incumbent."
